chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter is a craft table: paper strips, tiles, cut-out pieces, thread and clay. Making and fitting shapes shows which shapes fit together, what makes a triangle or a four-sided shape what it is, and how patterns repeat. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.title: Videos teach, tools explore
points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student weaves, fits, joins, folds and counts alone, with hints, retry and reset. Eleven tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own activities.

points.title: A tool in three steps
points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Every answerable question and activity of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

points.title: The pieces are on screen
points.text: The book's cut-out pieces (the rhombus with four triangles, the tangram, the regular shapes, the nets) are shown on screen, so every student has a full set to turn, flip and join.

points.title: No measuring of angles
points.text: The chapter compares angles by folding and by fitting pieces. It says right angle and equal angles and never measures an angle, and so does the plan.

tool_config.title: Mat Weaver
tool_config.idea: Feel what over and under mean by weaving paper strips across a mat with slits, and see that the words for a row come from what you wove: 1 under, 1 over, repeat, and the next row swaps. This is the free first try of the chapter, so it asks and shows; the video that follows names how to describe a row in words.
tool_config.screen: The craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A coloured paper mat with 8 upright slits (practice values) lies in the middle of the table and is the largest thing on screen. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. To the right of the mat a tray holds the 8 paper strips of your maths book, 4 blue and 4 yellow, each one longer than the mat is wide. The strip in hand lies across the first free row of the mat, and every place where it crosses a slit is a round tap spot. Controls: tap a crossing to switch it between over (the strip lies on top and shows its colour) and under (the strip goes below the slit paper and hides); an Alternate button that sets the whole strip to 1 under, 1 over, and so on; a Next strip button that fixes the strip and brings the next one from the tray; Undo, Hint, Retry (clears the strip in hand), Reset (clears the mat), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a row read-out in words under the mat that grows as the strip is woven, for example Row 1: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat), with the word repeat added once the same group has come twice; a counter strips woven out of 8; and a card number out of 6.
student_does: Think back to the woven baskets of the story, each one with its own weaving pattern. Look at the paper mat with 8 slits and the strip in hand. Tap one crossing twice to see the strip go over (it shows on top) and then under (it hides), then press Next.

Weave strip 1 going 1 under and 1 over, weave strip 2 going 1 over and 1 under, guess Row 3 before you weave it, press Alternate to finish all 8 strips, then press Reset and try a rule of your own (practice values: 2 over, 1 under).
Answer the open question of the story. Weave your own mat and describe Row 1 and Row 2 in words, as your maths book does.
challenges: Card 1: weave strip 1 across the 8 slits going 1 under and 1 over, again and again. Read the row read-out. Answer: the strip goes under slit 1, over slit 2, under slit 3, over slit 4, and so on, so it goes over slits 2, 4, 6 and 8: 4 overs and 4 unders, and 4 + 4 = 8 slits. The read-out says Row 1: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat).

Card 2: weave strip 2 across the next row going 1 over and 1 under, again and again. Compare it with the row above. Answer: strip 2 goes over slits 1, 3, 5 and 7, and the read-out says Row 2: 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). Row 2 does the opposite of Row 1: where Row 1 goes over, Row 2 goes under.

Card 3: guess first. What will Row 3 be if it swaps over and under in Row 2? Tap your guess, then weave strip 3. Answer: Row 3 is the same as Row 1, because swapping Row 1 gave Row 2 and swapping Row 2 gives Row 1 back: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat).

Card 4: press Alternate to weave strips 4 to 8, each strip doing the opposite of the strip above. How many strips are blue and how many are yellow? Answer: 4 blue and 4 yellow, because 4 + 4 = 8 strips. The odd rows go like Row 1 and the even rows go like Row 2, so the mat shows small checks.

Card 5 (practice values): press Reset. Weave Row 1 with a rule of your own: 2 over, 1 under, again and again, then weave Row 2 by swapping over and under. Answer: Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat) goes over, over, under, over, over, under, over, over across the 8 slits. Row 2 swaps it: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, 1 over, ... (repeat).

Challenge: 'We can describe the pattern of the above weave as follows.' Weave your own mat, then describe Row 1 and Row 2 in words. Answer: for the mat woven with 1 under and 1 over, Row 1: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat) and Row 2: 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). A rule of your own is fine too, if the words match what you wove. Your words may differ.
feedback: Tapping a crossing slides the strip over or under with a gentle movement, and the row read-out adds the step in words.
A second strip that does the opposite of the row above gets a soft green note: This strip goes over where the last one goes under: the rows swap.
A strip that copies the row above gets a soft amber note: This strip goes over where the strip above goes over. Look again: should this row swap?
Alternate fills a strip with the pattern and says: 1 under, 1 over, again and again. Read the words in the read-out.
When the student describes a row that does not match the read-out, the tool shows the row with each step numbered and says: Count the steps that stay together. It never shows a red cross.
tool_config.done_when: Strips 1 and 2 are woven with the rows swapped, all 8 strips are woven, the student has woven and read a row of their own rule, and has described Row 1 and Row 2 of their own mat in words.

hint_ladder.text: What does the strip in hand do at each slit: does it lie on top, or go below the slit paper? Look at the first crossing and tap it.
Go slit by slit. For Row 1 the strip goes under, then over, then under, then over. Say the steps out loud as you tap.
For Row 1 tap slit 1 for under, slit 2 for over, slit 3 for under, and keep going to slit 8. The read-out should say 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat).
Press Alternate. The strip weaves itself: under, over, under, over across the 8 slits. Now read the read-out and say the row in your own words.

content.text:
Let us make paper mats. You will need: A coloured paper (30 cm long and 20 cm wide) and eight paper strips of two different colours (3 cm wide and longer than 20 cm).
Fold the coloured paper in half along the longer side.
Draw vertical lines at equal distances from the closed end and cut slits leaving a gap of 3 cm at the top.
Carefully unfold the paper. There will be no cuts in the paper at the top and the bottom.
Take one colour strip and weave it across the slits going 1 under and 1 over, and again 1 under and 1 over. Repeat it for the first row.
Take one more strip of another colour and weave it across the slits going 1 over and 1 under, and again 1 over and 1 under. Repeat it for the second row.
Weave all the strips in the same alternating pattern. Neatly fold any extra strip ends behind the mat. Your mat is ready!
We can describe the pattern of the above weave as follows. Row 1: 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, ... (repeat). Row 2: 1 over, 1 under, 1 over, 1 under, ... (repeat).

content.text:
1. Predict first: a strip goes over, over, over, under, under, and then does the same again. How can you tell a friend this row in a few words, without saying every slit?
2. Count the steps that stay together: 3 over, then 2 under. Over means the strip lies on top and shows. Under means it goes below.
3. That group comes again and again, so we say repeat. The row is: 3 over, 2 under (repeat).
4. The next row swaps over and under. Where Row 1 goes over, Row 2 goes under. So Row 2 is: 3 under, 2 over (repeat).
5. Your maths book weaves a paper mat this way. The slits are cut in a paper 30 cm long, with a gap of 3 cm at the top and the bottom, so the slits are 30 − 3 − 3 = 24 cm long. Eight strips that are 3 cm wide fill them: 8 × 3 = 24 cm.
6. Rule: describe a row by counting the over and under steps, then say repeat.

content.text:
Worked example: A mat has 10 slits. A strip goes over, over, over, under, under, over, over, over, under, under. Describe Row 1 in words. Then describe Row 2, where every strip swaps over and under.
1. Read the strip slit by slit: over, over, over, under, under, over, over, over, under, under. Over means the strip lies on top and shows.
2. Count the steps that stay together: 3 over, then 2 under.
3. The same group comes again, so the row repeats: Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat).
4. Row 2 swaps over and under: every over becomes under and every under becomes over.
5. So Row 2 goes under, under, under, over, over, under, under, under, over, over: Row 2: 3 under, 2 over (repeat).
6. Check: each group has 3 + 2 = 5 slits, and two groups make 5 + 5 = 10 slits, the whole row.
Answer: Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat). Row 2: 3 under, 2 over (repeat)

content.text:
1. Predict first: a mat has 9 slits and Row 1 is 1 over, 2 under (repeat). Each next row is the row above moved one slit to the right. After how many rows will a row look the same as Row 1?
2. Write Row 1: over, under, under, over, under, under, over, under, under.
3. Move it one slit to the right. The last step comes round to the front. Row 2 is under, over, under, under, over, under, under, over, under.
4. Move it again for Row 3, and again for Row 4. After each move, compare the new row with Row 1.
5. Row 4 is the same as Row 1, so the rows repeat after 3 rows. Row 5 is the same as Row 2, and Row 6 is the same as Row 3.

tool_config.title: Weave Rules
tool_config.idea: Build the rows of a weave from rule cards (a count, over or under, repeat) and find the row where the pattern starts to repeat. The cards make the rule itself the thing that students handle, so long rules and many rows are quick to try.
tool_config.screen: A weaving frame with 16 columns on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The grid of crossings, 16 columns wide, is the largest thing on screen: in each row a crossing shows the strip colour where the strip goes over and cream where it goes under. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Above each row sits a rule line where cards are dropped in order. A shelf under the frame holds the rule cards: the number cards 1, 2 and 3, the word cards over and under, a card (repeat) and a card (do not repeat). A small target card on the right shows the mat to copy when a challenge gives one. The frame can show 10, 12 or 16 slits: the cards of a challenge set the number. Controls: drag cards into the rule line of a row in order, for example 2, over, 1, under, (repeat); a Weave button that colours the row from its cards; a Rows repeat from here button to tap on the row that is the same as Row 1; Undo, Hint, Retry (clears the row being built), Reset (clears the frame), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: a row list on the left that gives every woven row in words, for example Row 3: 2 under, 1 over (repeat); a slit counter for the row being built (for example 10 of 10 slits); the number of rows woven; a marker under the row chosen as the repeat; and a card number out of 6.
student_does: Look at the row from the video, Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat), woven on 10 slits, and at Row 2 that swaps it (practice values). Tap a card of the rule line to see which slits it covers, then press Next.

Build rows from the cards (practice values), swap a row, then weave three rows where each row is the row above moved one slit to the right, and tap the row that is the same as Row 1. Say after how many rows the pattern repeats.
Weave the four rules of your maths book and say when the pattern repeats, then work out the steps of a design until it starts repeating.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values, 12 slits): build Row 1 from the cards: 1 over, 3 under (repeat). Press Weave. How many slits go over and how many go under? Answer: the row goes over, under, under, under, over, under, under, under, over, under, under, under, so 3 slits go over and 9 go under, and 3 + 9 = 12.

Card 2 (practice values, 12 slits): build Row 2 so that it swaps over and under in Row 1. Answer: Row 2: 1 under, 3 over (repeat), which goes under, over, over, over, under, over, over, over, under, over, over, over.

Card 3 (practice values, 12 slits): build Row 1: 2 over, 1 under (repeat). Then build Row 2 as Row 1 moved one slit to the right, so that the last step comes round to the front. Answer: Row 2: 1 under (do not repeat), 2 over, 1 under (repeat), which goes under, over, over, under, over, over, under, over, over, under, over, over.

Card 4 (practice values, 12 slits): build Row 3 and Row 4 in the same way, each one moved one slit to the right. Which row is the same as Row 1? Tap Rows repeat from here on it. Answer: Row 3: 1 over (do not repeat), 1 under, 2 over (repeat). Row 4 is the same as Row 1: 2 over, 1 under (repeat). The rows repeat from Row 4, after 3 rows.

Challenge: 'Try to weave a pattern, using the rules given below. Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). Row 2: 1 under (do not repeat), 3 over, 3 under, 3 over, 3 under, ... (repeat). Row 3: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, ... (repeat). Row 4: 1 over (do not repeat), 3 under, 3 over ... (repeat). Continue weaving in this order.' Build the four rows on 16 slits, then keep weaving. When does the pattern repeat? Answer: Row 3 swaps over and under in Row 1 and Row 4 swaps Row 2, and Row 5 follows the first rule again, so it is the same as Row 1. The pattern repeats after 4 rows.

Challenge: 'Can you work out the steps for any of these designs and weave the pattern? Write the steps of the pattern in your notebook for each row until it starts repeating.' Choose the design on the target card, read it row by row, and build each row from the cards, so that the row list is your notebook. Answer: for the design of purple strips on 16 slits, Row 1: 1 under (do not repeat), 3 over, 3 under (repeat), then Rows 2 to 6 follow the target card, and Row 7 is the same as Row 1, so it repeats after 6 rows. The design of teal and lavender repeats after 4 rows. Your row list may differ in which design you choose.
feedback: A row built from cards is woven with a gentle slide and the row list adds its words, for example Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat).
If the row does not fill the slits, a soft amber note says how many slits are left, for example: Your row covers 9 of 10 slits: one more step is needed.
A row that swaps over and under in the row above gets a soft green note: Row 3 swaps over and under in Row 1: 2 under, 1 over.

When a row is tapped as the repeat but is not the same as Row 1, the tool lays the two rows one over the other and shows the first slit where they differ, in soft amber. It says: Not the same as Row 1 yet. Move on to the next row.
When a row starts its pattern in the same place as the row above, the tool says: Each new row can begin at a different place in the pattern. Compare where the first group starts.
tool_config.done_when: The rows of every card are built from cards and woven, the repeat is found on the rows of practice values and on the four rules, and the student has written the steps of a design until it repeats.

media.description: Concept video: Show how to describe a weave row in words with over and under steps and the word repeat, and that the next row swaps over and under. It works this example: A mat has 10 slits. A strip goes over, over, over, under, under, over, over, over, under, under. Describe Row 1 in words. Then describe Row 2, where every strip swaps over and under.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a strip goes over, over, over, under, under, and then does the same again. How can you tell a friend this row in a few words, without saying every slit? Count the steps that stay together: 3 over, then 2 under. Over means the strip lies on top and shows. Under means it goes below. That group comes again and again, so we say repeat. The row is: 3 over, 2 under (repeat). The next row swaps over and under. Where Row 1 goes over, Row 2 goes under. So Row 2 is: 3 under, 2 over (repeat). Your maths book weaves a paper mat this way. The slits are cut in a paper 30 cm long, with a gap of 3 cm at the top and the bottom, so the slits are 30 − 3 − 3 = 24 cm long. Eight strips that are 3 cm wide fill them: 8 × 3 = 24 cm. Rule: describe a row by counting the over and under steps, then say repeat. 1. Read the strip slit by slit: over, over, over, under, under, over, over, over, under, under. Over means the strip lies on top and shows. 2. Count the steps that stay together: 3 over, then 2 under. 3. The same group comes again, so the row repeats: Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat). 4. Row 2 swaps over and under: every over becomes under and every under becomes over. 5. So Row 2 goes under, under, under, over, over, under, under, under, over, over: Row 2: 3 under, 2 over (repeat). 6. Check: each group has 3 + 2 = 5 slits, and two groups make 5 + 5 = 10 slits, the whole row. Answer: Row 1: 3 over, 2 under (repeat). Row 2: 3 under, 2 over (repeat)

steps: Over means the strip lies on top and shows. Under means it goes below.
Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). The strip goes over, over, under again and again.
Row 2: say 1 under once (do not repeat), then 3 over, 3 under, 3 over, 3 under, ... (repeat).
Row 3: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, ... (repeat). This swaps over and under in Row 1.
Row 4: say 1 over once (do not repeat), then 3 under, 3 over, ... (repeat). This swaps over and under in Row 2.
Row 5 follows the first rule again, so it is the same as Row 1. The pattern repeats after 4 rows.
Check: 4 rows repeated 4 times make 4 × 4 = 16 rows, the whole mat.

media.teaching_notes: 1. Over means the strip lies on top and shows. Under means it goes below. 2. Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). The strip goes over, over, under again and again. 3. Row 2: say 1 under once (do not repeat), then 3 over, 3 under, 3 over, 3 under, ... (repeat). 4. Row 3: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, ... (repeat). This swaps over and under in Row 1. 5. Row 4: say 1 over once (do not repeat), then 3 under, 3 over, ... (repeat). This swaps over and under in Row 2. 6. Row 5 follows the first rule again, so it is the same as Row 1. The pattern repeats after 4 rows. 7. Check: 4 rows repeated 4 times make 4 × 4 = 16 rows, the whole mat. Answer: Sample answer: Row 1: 2 over, 1 under; Row 2: 1 under, then 3 over, 3 under; Row 3 swaps Row 1; Row 4 swaps Row 2. Row 5 is Row 1: it repeats after 4 rows. Your answer may differ.

steps: The design is a mat 21 squares across and 21 squares down. A yellow square is a strip that shows on top.
Top row: a yellow square sits on every other cell, starting with the first, so there are 11 yellow squares and 10 gaps: 11 + 10 = 21.
The first column and the last column also have a yellow square on every other cell.
From the top row, the squares then spread in two diagonal lines, like the sides of a diamond.
The left half and the right half of the design match, so draw one half and copy it on the other side.
Check: every row has 21 cells, and the part already drawn on the grid matches your drawing.

modules.module_summary: Regular shapes, which regular shapes fit round a point with no gap and no overlap, and patterns made of two shapes.

segments.summary: Shapes that have equal sides are called regular shapes. Shapes fit around a point when their corners fill the space with no gap and no overlap, and then they tessellate.

content.text:
We often use tiles of the same shape or a combination of shapes to cover a region.
You can see pentagons (5-sided figures) in this figure. As all its sides are equal it is a regular pentagon.
Shapes that have equal sides are called regular shapes.
A regular octagon means a shape with eight equal sides.
Regular octagons do not tessellate.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a square has every side 6 cm and a rectangle is 6 cm by 4 cm. Which one is a regular shape?
2. Look at the sides. The square has 4 equal sides, so it is a regular shape. The rectangle has sides of 6 cm and 4 cm, so its sides are not all equal.
3. A pentagon is a 5-sided shape. With all 5 sides equal, 3 cm each, it is a regular pentagon.
4. A regular octagon is a shape with 8 equal sides.
5. We use tiles of one shape, or of a few shapes, to cover a region. Soon you will see which regular shapes fit together.
6. Rule: shapes that have equal sides are called regular shapes.

content.text:
Worked example: A square has every side 6 cm. A rectangle is 6 cm by 4 cm. A pentagon has every side 3 cm. Which of these shapes are regular shapes?
1. A regular shape has all its sides equal.
2. The square: all 4 sides are 6 cm. They are equal, so it is a regular shape.
3. The rectangle: 2 sides are 6 cm and 2 sides are 4 cm. They are not all equal, so it is not a regular shape.
4. The pentagon: all 5 sides are 3 cm. They are equal, so it is a regular pentagon.
5. Check: in the square and in the pentagon every side is the same length, but the rectangle has a longer pair of sides and a shorter pair.
Answer: The square and the pentagon are regular shapes. The rectangle is not, because its sides are not all equal

content.text:
Pentagons cannot fill a region without leaving gaps. So, we say that regular pentagons do not tessellate.
Regular triangles when fitted around a point leave no gaps and there is no overlap.
Triangles with all equal sides are also called equilateral triangles. Therefore, equilateral triangles tessellate.

lines: Pentagons cannot fill a region without leaving gaps. So, we say that regular pentagons do not tessellate.
Regular triangles when fitted around a point leave no gaps and there is no overlap.
Triangles with all equal sides are also called equilateral triangles. Therefore, equilateral triangles tessellate.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have rectangles of one size, 6 cm by 4 cm, and each has 4 right angle corners. How many can you fit around a point with no gap and no overlap?
2. Put one corner of each rectangle on the point. After 4 rectangles the 4 right angle corners fill all the space round the point.
3. A 5th rectangle has no room. It would lie over the others. That is an overlap.
4. Watch for two things when shapes meet at a point: a gap that is left, and an overlap.
5. Pentagons cannot fill a region without leaving gaps. The gap left is too small for another pentagon, and a pentagon put there would overlap. So regular pentagons do not tessellate.
6. Regular triangles fitted around a point leave no gaps and there is no overlap. Triangles with all equal sides are equilateral triangles. So equilateral triangles tessellate.
7. Rule: shapes fit around a point when their corners fill the space with no gap and no overlap. If a gap is left that is too small for another shape, or a shape overlaps, they do not fit.

content.text:
Worked example: Rectangles of one size, 6 cm by 4 cm, each have 4 right angle corners. Put one corner of each rectangle on a point, edge to edge. How many rectangles fit around the point with no gap and no overlap? Would a 5th rectangle fit?
1. Put one corner of the first rectangle on the point. Each corner of a rectangle is a right angle.
2. Put the second rectangle next to it, edge to edge, with one corner on the point too.
3. Go on round the point. After 4 rectangles the 4 right angle corners fill the whole space.
4. There is no gap and no overlap, so 4 rectangles fit around the point.
5. Try a 5th rectangle. There is no space left, so it would lie over the others. That is an overlap.
6. Check: 4 corners fill the space exactly, so 3 rectangles would leave a gap and 5 would overlap.
Answer: 4 rectangles fit around the point with no gap and no overlap, because 4 right angle corners fill the space. A 5th would overlap

If the gap left is too small for another shape, or a shape would overlap, they do not fit.

tool_config.idea: Fit regular triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons and octagons around a point and count how many fit, watching for the gap and the overlap: some shapes fill the space exactly, and others leave a gap that is too small to use.
tool_config.screen: A tile mat on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A cream mat with one orange point marked in the middle is the largest thing on screen, and the shapes are placed on it. On a shelf at the left sit cutouts of five shapes, each with every side the same length: an equilateral triangle, a square, a regular pentagon, a regular hexagon and a regular octagon. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a shape so that one corner sits on the marked point; the shape turns and snaps edge to edge to the shape before it; Undo; Hint; Retry (clears the mat); Reset (clears the mat and the counter); Back and Next in the same places on every card. A gap that is left glows soft amber, and a shape that lies over another shows its overlap glowing soft amber. Read-outs: a counter shapes at the point (for example 3), a status line that says gap left, no gap, or overlap, a note that tells whether the gap left is big enough for one more of the shape in hand, and a card number out of 7.
student_does: Which regular shape did you meet in the video, a shape with all its sides equal? Take the square from the shelf and put one corner on the point. Then press Next.

Fit triangles, squares and hexagons round the point and count how many fit; fit pentagons and see the gap that is too small; fit octagons, and then try a square in the gap (practice values for the square).
Answer the book's questions about five squares and about regular hexagons, using the mat to check your answer.
challenges: Card 1: fit equilateral triangles round the point, edge to edge, until the space is full. How many fit? Answer: 6 triangles fit, with no gap and no overlap.
Card 2: fit squares round the point. How many fit? Answer: 4 squares fit, with no gap and no overlap, because 4 right angle corners fill the space.
Card 3: fit regular hexagons round the point. How many fit? Answer: 3 hexagons fit, with no gap and no overlap.

Card 4: fit regular pentagons round the point. How many fit, and can one more go in the gap? Answer: 3 pentagons fit and a gap is left. The gap is too small for a 4th pentagon, which would overlap, so regular pentagons do not tessellate.

Card 5 (practice values for the square): fit regular octagons round the point, then try a square in the gap. Answer: 2 octagons fit side by side and the gap is too small for a 3rd octagon, which would overlap. A square fits the gap exactly, so 2 octagons and 1 square fill the point.

Challenge: 'Can five squares fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?' Try it on the mat. Answer: no. 4 squares already fill the space round the point, so a fifth square would overlap the first one.

Challenge: 'Can regular hexagons (6-sided shapes with equal sides) fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Try and see. How many fit together at a point?' Answer: yes. 3 regular hexagons fit together at a point with no gap and no overlap.
feedback: When the corners fill the space, the glow turns soft green and the status line says: No gap, no overlap. 6 triangles fit.
When the space is not full, the gap glows soft amber and the note says how it compares with one more shape, for example: The gap is too small for another pentagon.
When a shape would lie over another, the part that overlaps glows soft amber and the note says: A fifth square would overlap the first: 4 squares fill the space.
A shape dropped far from the point slides back with a clue: Put one corner of the shape on the marked point.
A small gap is never accepted as fitting: the tool says: A gap is left, so this shape does not tessellate by itself. It never shows a red cross.

media.description: Concept video: Explain that shapes with all sides equal are regular shapes, with a square, a pentagon and a rectangle that is not regular. It works this example: A square has every side 6 cm. A rectangle is 6 cm by 4 cm. A pentagon has every side 3 cm. Which of these shapes are regular shapes?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a square has every side 6 cm and a rectangle is 6 cm by 4 cm. Which one is a regular shape? Look at the sides. The square has 4 equal sides, so it is a regular shape. The rectangle has sides of 6 cm and 4 cm, so its sides are not all equal. A pentagon is a 5-sided shape. With all 5 sides equal, 3 cm each, it is a regular pentagon. A regular octagon is a shape with 8 equal sides. We use tiles of one shape, or of a few shapes, to cover a region. Soon you will see which regular shapes fit together. Rule: shapes that have equal sides are called regular shapes. 1. A regular shape has all its sides equal. 2. The square: all 4 sides are 6 cm. They are equal, so it is a regular shape. 3. The rectangle: 2 sides are 6 cm and 2 sides are 4 cm. They are not all equal, so it is not a regular shape. 4. The pentagon: all 5 sides are 3 cm. They are equal, so it is a regular pentagon. 5. Check: in the square and in the pentagon every side is the same length, but the rectangle has a longer pair of sides and a shorter pair. Answer: The square and the pentagon are regular shapes. The rectangle is not, because its sides are not all equal

media.description: Concept video: Show that shapes fit round a point when their corners fill the space with no gap and no overlap, and that such shapes tessellate. It works this example: Rectangles of one size, 6 cm by 4 cm, each have 4 right angle corners. Put one corner of each rectangle on a point, edge to edge. How many rectangles fit around the point with no gap and no overlap? Would a 5th rectangle fit?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: you have rectangles of one size, 6 cm by 4 cm, and each has 4 right angle corners. How many can you fit around a point with no gap and no overlap? Put one corner of each rectangle on the point. After 4 rectangles the 4 right angle corners fill all the space round the point. A 5th rectangle has no room. It would lie over the others. That is an overlap. Watch for two things when shapes meet at a point: a gap that is left, and an overlap. Pentagons cannot fill a region without leaving gaps. The gap left is too small for another pentagon, and a pentagon put there would overlap. So regular pentagons do not tessellate. Regular triangles fitted around a point leave no gaps and there is no overlap. Triangles with all equal sides are equilateral triangles. So equilateral triangles tessellate. Rule: shapes fit around a point when their corners fill the space with no gap and no overlap. If a gap is left that is too small for another shape, or a shape overlaps, they do not fit. 1. Put one corner of the first rectangle on the point. Each corner of a rectangle is a right angle. 2. Put the second rectangle next to it, edge to edge, with one corner on the point too. 3. Go on round the point. After 4 rectangles the 4 right angle corners fill the whole space. 4. There is no gap and no overlap, so 4 rectangles fit around the point. 5. Try a 5th rectangle. There is no space left, so it would lie over the others. That is an overlap. 6. Check: 4 corners fill the space exactly, so 3 rectangles would leave a gap and 5 would overlap. Answer: 4 rectangles fit around the point with no gap and no overlap, because 4 right angle corners fill the space. A 5th would overlap

content.question: We have placed 3 pentagons around a point. Can we fit one more into the empty space?
steps: Look at the 3 pentagons that meet at the point. Their corners fill most of the space round the point.
The empty space that is left is smaller than one more pentagon corner.
A fourth pentagon is too big for the gap. It would lie over its neighbours: an overlap.
So regular pentagons leave a gap that is too small to use, and they do not tessellate.
Check: a fourth pentagon would stick out over the others, so the answer is no.
content.answer: No. The gap is too small for a fourth pentagon, so it would overlap the others. Regular pentagons do not tessellate.

content.text: Here is a tessellating pattern with more than one shape.
content.publication_text: Here is a tessellating pattern with more than one shape.
lines: Here is a tessellating pattern with more than one shape.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a border has 12 tiles in a row: square, triangle, square, triangle, and so on. How many squares and how many triangles are there?
2. The tiles take turns, so every second tile is a square: 6 squares and 6 triangles. 6 + 6 = 12.
3. Look at each join between two neighbours. A square is on one side and a triangle is on the other.
4. So the same two kinds of shape meet at every join: a square and a triangle.
5. A pattern with two shapes repeats the shapes in the same order. If the order changes, the shapes at a join can change too.
6. Rule: tiles of two shapes can cover a region when they repeat in the same order. At each meeting point, list the shapes and compare.

content.text:
Worked example: A border has 12 tiles in a row. The tiles go square, triangle, square, triangle, and so on. How many squares and how many triangles are there, and which shapes meet at every join?
1. The tiles take turns: square, triangle, square, triangle, ... The first tile is a square.
2. Every second tile is a square, so there are 12 ÷ 2 = 6 squares.
3. The other tiles are triangles: 12 − 6 = 6 triangles.
4. Check the count: 6 + 6 = 12 tiles.
5. Look at each join between two neighbours. Every join has a square on one side and a triangle on the other.
6. So the same two kinds of shape meet at every join: a square and a triangle.
7. Check: the tiles never put two squares or two triangles side by side, because they take turns.
Answer: 6 squares and 6 triangles, because 6 + 6 = 12. At every join a square and a triangle meet, the same set each time

tool_config.title: Pattern Tiler
tool_config.idea: Continue a pattern made of two shapes and list the shapes that meet at a point. Placing the tiles is the pattern, and the meeting-point list makes the question whether the same set of shapes meets at every point something that can be seen.
tool_config.screen: A floor of dots on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A board with a dot grid is the largest thing on screen: a triangle dot grid for hexagons and triangles, and a square dot grid for squares, octagons and tilted squares. On a shelf at the left sit cutouts of a regular hexagon, an equilateral triangle, a regular octagon, a square, and the tilted square and the triangle with two equal sides that your maths book uses in its last pattern. Four or five marked points sit on the board when a card asks about them. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a tile, turn it with the Turn button, and it snaps to the dots and to the tile next to it; tap a marked point to open the checker list; a colour tool with purple, yellow, green, blue and orange; Undo; Hint; Retry (clears the last tiles placed); Reset (clears the board); Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the checker list for a tapped point, written as a count for each shape, for example 2 octagons, 1 square; a line that says same set or different set when two points are compared; and a card number out of 6.
student_does: Look at the border of squares and triangles from the video, where the two shapes take turns. Tap one join and read the list of shapes that meet there, then press Next.

Continue a border of squares and triangles (practice values), fill hexagons and triangles round a point, read the list at two points and compare them, then look at a border where the shapes do not take turns.
Answer the book's questions about the pattern of octagons and squares, and about the pattern of hexagons and triangles.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): a border starts with 4 tiles: square, triangle, square, triangle. Place 4 more tiles to make a border of 8 tiles. How many squares and how many triangles are there? Answer: the tiles go square, triangle, square, triangle, square, triangle, square, triangle: 4 squares and 4 triangles, and 4 + 4 = 8.

Card 2: on the triangle dot grid, place hexagons and triangles round one point until the space is full. Answer: 2 hexagons and 2 triangles fill the point with no gap and no overlap, in the order hexagon, triangle, hexagon, triangle.

Card 3: tap two points of your pattern and read the checker lists. Are the same shapes meeting at both? Answer: at both points 2 hexagons and 2 triangles meet, so the same set of shapes meets at both points.

Card 4 (practice values): the tool shows a border that goes square, triangle, triangle, square, triangle, triangle, and so on. Tap three joins and compare the lists. Answer: one join has a square and a triangle, the next has two triangles, and the next has a triangle and a square, so the same set does not meet at every join, because the shapes do not take turns.

Challenge: 'Look at the pattern given below. What shapes are coming together at the marked points? Are the same set of shapes coming together at these points? Continue the pattern and colour it appropriately.' The board shows 4 rows of 4 regular octagons with a small square between each group of four. Answer: 2 octagons and 1 square come together at each marked point, and yes, it is the same set every time. Continue with octagons edge to edge and a small square wherever four octagons meet. Your colours may differ.

A point where the tiles leave a gap glows soft amber with the note: A gap is left here. Which shape would fill it? A small gap is not accepted as fitting.
A tile put in the wrong place slides back with a clue, for example: Put the square where four octagons meet. The tool never shows a red cross.

content.book_number: Tessellation Patterns: are the triangles equilateral
content.question: Here is a tiling pattern made using two different shapes, squares and triangles. Are the triangles equilateral? Why or why not?
steps: An equilateral triangle has all 3 sides equal. Compare the sides of one triangle by counting along the dots.
Two sides of the triangle are as long as a side of a square, a little more than 2 grid steps.
The third side is shorter. It is exactly 2 grid steps.
So two sides are equal and the third side is not.
Check: for an equilateral triangle all 3 sides must be equal, and here the third side is shorter.
content.answer: No. Two sides of each triangle are as long as a side of a square, and the third side is shorter, so the triangles are not equilateral.
content.text:
1. An equilateral triangle has all $3$ sides equal. Compare the sides of one triangle by counting along the dots.
2. Two sides of the triangle are as long as a side of a square, a little more than $2$ grid steps.

modules.module_summary: Making triangles and four-sided shapes from the pieces of a rhombus, the seven tangram pieces, and telling square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram apart.

segments.summary: A rhombus has all sides equal, and it can be divided into four triangles. Two of these pieces can be joined to make a triangle. An isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides and 2 equal angles, an equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles, and a scalene triangle has no equal sides and no equal angles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: triangle A has sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. Triangle B has sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. Triangle C has sides 8 cm, 8 cm and 3 cm. Which one has all 3 angles equal, and which one has no equal angles?
2. Count the equal sides first. A has 3 equal sides, so A is an equilateral triangle. Fold A in half through any corner: the two halves lie exactly on each other and the other 2 corners land on each other, so all 3 angles are equal.
3. B has no equal sides, so B is a scalene triangle. Fold B in half through each corner: the two halves never lie exactly on each other, so no two angles are equal.
4. C has 2 equal sides, so C is an isosceles triangle with 2 equal angles.
5. You can compare the angles of any shape by folding paper: angles that land exactly on each other are equal.
6. Rule: 3 equal sides means equilateral, 2 equal sides means isosceles and no equal sides means scalene; equal sides go with equal angles.

content.text:
Worked example: Triangle A has sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. Triangle B has sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. Triangle C has sides 8 cm, 8 cm and 3 cm. Name each triangle and say how many of its angles are equal.
1. Triangle A: the sides are 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. All 3 sides are equal, so A is an equilateral triangle.
2. Fold A in half through a corner, so that the two halves lie on each other. They match through every corner, so all 3 angles of A are equal.
3. Triangle B: the sides are 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. No two sides are equal, so B is a scalene triangle.
4. Fold B in half through each of its corners. The two halves never lie exactly on each other, so no two angles of B are equal.
5. Triangle C: the sides are 8 cm, 8 cm and 3 cm. Two sides are equal, so C is an isosceles triangle with 2 equal angles.
6. Check: A has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles, C has 2 and 2, and B has none and none. The number of equal sides and the number of equal angles always match.
Answer: A is equilateral (3 equal sides, 3 equal angles), B is scalene (no equal sides, no equal angles), C is isosceles (2 equal sides, 2 equal angles)

tool_config.title: Triangle Check
tool_config.idea: Sort triangles made from the pieces of a rhombus by what you measure and fold: measure the sides with a ruler, fold to compare the angles, and see that equal sides go with equal angles. A triangle with 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles is equilateral, with 2 equal sides and 2 equal angles isosceles, and with no equal sides and no equal angles scalene. This tool measures and folds triangles that are given; it does not join pieces.
tool_config.screen: The craft table seen from above, a warm wooden table drawn as a polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A big paper triangle lies in the middle of the table and is the largest thing on screen. Along the left edge is a tray of 4 paper triangles made from the pieces of the rhombus, each with a number tag from 1 to 4: triangle 1 is 2 pieces joined along their middle sides (3 equal sides), triangle 2 is 2 pieces joined along their shortest sides (a wider triangle with 2 equal sides), triangle 3 is a single piece, and triangle 4 is 4 pieces joined into one big triangle. Tap a triangle in the tray to bring it to the middle. A wooden ruler lies across the top of the table. Drag the ruler onto a side, or tap a side, and the ruler slides along that side and a tag on the ruler shows its length. The ruler reads to the nearest whole cm, and the shortest side of a piece reads 4 cm, so the middle side of a piece reads about 7 cm and the longest side reads 8 cm (practice values). Beside the table a side list with 3 boxes shows the lengths measured so far for this triangle, and two boxes that hold the same number glow green with an equals sign between them. A Fold button sits under the triangle: tap a corner to choose it, and it glows orange; then tap Fold, and the triangle folds along the line from that corner to the middle of the opposite side. A fold read-out in words says whether the two halves match, and the corners that landed on each other show matching arcs, drawn in green when they match. An Unfold button opens the triangle again. A Halve button, switched on only for the book's questions, splits the triangle along the line from the chosen corner to the middle of the opposite side and slides the two halves apart so that the ruler can measure each half. Along the bottom edge are 3 sorting trays labelled Equilateral, Isosceles and Scalene. Drag a triangle into a tray; a tray takes a triangle only after its 3 sides are measured. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Hint, Retry (returns the triangle in the middle to its first state), Reset (returns all 4 triangles and clears the trays and the side list), Undo (takes back the last move), Back and Next are in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the side list, the number of equal sides found, the fold read-out, the tray counter (for example sorted 2 of 4), and the card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the 2 triangles you made from 2 pieces in the video, triangle 1 with 3 equal sides and the wider triangle 2. Tap each one and say how many of its sides you think are equal, then press Next.

For each of the 4 triangles, measure the 3 sides with the ruler, fold the triangle from each corner, and drag it into the tray it belongs in. See that the number of equal sides is also the number of equal angles.

Answer 2 questions from your maths book: how many different types of triangles you can make from 2 pieces and what you notice about their sides, and how many sides of each half are equal when you halve the equilateral triangle.
challenges: Card 1: triangle 1 (2 pieces joined along their middle sides). Tap each of its 3 sides to measure it. What do the 3 sides read? Answer: 8 cm, 8 cm and 8 cm (practice values), so all 3 sides are equal.

Card 2: fold triangle 1 from each of its 3 corners. What happens? Answer: the two halves match from every corner, so all 3 angles are equal. Triangle 1 has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles: it is an equilateral triangle.

Card 3: triangle 2 (2 pieces joined along their shortest sides). Measure its 3 sides and fold it from each corner. Answer: the sides read 8 cm, 8 cm and about 14 cm (practice values), so 2 sides are equal. The halves match only when you fold from the corner between the 2 equal sides, so 2 angles are equal. It is an isosceles triangle.

Card 4: triangle 3 (a single piece). Measure its 3 sides and fold it from each corner. Answer: the sides read 4 cm, about 7 cm and 8 cm (practice values), so no 2 sides are equal. The halves never match, so no 2 angles are equal. It is a scalene triangle.

Card 5: measure triangle 4 (4 pieces joined into one big triangle), then drag all 4 triangles into the trays. Answer: triangle 1 goes to Equilateral, triangle 2 to Isosceles, and triangles 3 and 4 to Scalene. Triangle 4 reads 8 cm, about 14 cm and 16 cm (practice values), so no 2 of its sides are equal.

Challenge: 'How many different types of triangles can you make? Now, observe and measure the sides of these triangles. What do you notice?' Use triangles 1 and 2, which are made from 2 pieces. Answer: 2 types from 2 pieces: one with all 3 sides equal and a wider one with 2 equal sides. In both triangles, 2 sides are equal.

Challenge: 'Now, cut the equilateral triangle in half. How many sides of each new triangle are equal?' Press Halve on triangle 1 and measure each half. Answer: none. The 3 sides of each half read 4 cm, about 7 cm and 8 cm (practice values), all different, so each half is a scalene triangle.

A fold that matches shows the two halves lying on each other, matching arcs in green and the words: The two halves match, so these 2 angles are equal. A fold that does not match shows a soft amber note: The halves do not match from this corner. Try another corner.

media.description: Concept video: Explain isosceles triangles: 2 equal sides and 2 equal angles, checked by folding. It works this example: A triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm. Is it an isosceles triangle? Fold it in half and say what you notice about its angles.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a triangle has sides 5 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm. Fold it in half so that the two 5 cm sides lie on each other. Will the two angles at the ends of the 3 cm side match too? A rhombus is a shape with all sides equal. It can be divided into four triangles, and 2 of these triangles can be joined to make a new triangle. A triangle with 2 equal sides is called an isosceles triangle. Now fold the triangle. The two 5 cm sides lie exactly on each other, and the two angles at the ends of the 3 cm side land on each other too. They match. So an isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides and also 2 equal angles. Rule: an isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides and 2 equal angles; fold it in half to check. 1. Compare the sides: 5 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm. Two sides are equal (5 cm and 5 cm) and the third side is different (3 cm). 2. A triangle with 2 equal sides is an isosceles triangle, so this is an isosceles triangle. 3. Fold it in half through the corner where the two 5 cm sides meet, so that the two 5 cm sides lie on each other. 4. The two halves match exactly. The two corners at the ends of the 3 cm side land on each other. 5. So the two angles at the ends of the 3 cm side are equal. 6. Check: the fold splits the triangle into two halves that match, so equal sides and equal angles come as a pair. Answer: Yes, it is an isosceles triangle: it has 2 equal sides (5 cm and 5 cm). When it is folded in half the two halves match, so it also has 2 equal angles

media.description: Concept video: Explain equilateral triangles (3 equal sides and angles) and scalene triangles (no equal sides). It works this example: Triangle A has sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. Triangle B has sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. Triangle C has sides 8 cm, 8 cm and 3 cm. Name each triangle and say how many of its angles are equal.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: triangle A has sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. Triangle B has sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. Triangle C has sides 8 cm, 8 cm and 3 cm. Which one has all 3 angles equal, and which one has no equal angles? Count the equal sides first. A has 3 equal sides, so A is an equilateral triangle. Fold A in half through any corner: the two halves lie exactly on each other and the other 2 corners land on each other, so all 3 angles are equal. B has no equal sides, so B is a scalene triangle. Fold B in half through each corner: the two halves never lie exactly on each other, so no two angles are equal. C has 2 equal sides, so C is an isosceles triangle with 2 equal angles. You can compare the angles of any shape by folding paper: angles that land exactly on each other are equal. Rule: 3 equal sides means equilateral, 2 equal sides means isosceles and no equal sides means scalene; equal sides go with equal angles. 1. Triangle A: the sides are 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. All 3 sides are equal, so A is an equilateral triangle. 2. Fold A in half through a corner, so that the two halves lie on each other. They match through every corner, so all 3 angles of A are equal. 3. Triangle B: the sides are 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. No two sides are equal, so B is a scalene triangle. 4. Fold B in half through each of its corners. The two halves never lie exactly on each other, so no two angles of B are equal. 5. Triangle C: the sides are 8 cm, 8 cm and 3 cm. Two sides are equal, so C is an isosceles triangle with 2 equal angles. 6. Check: A has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles, C has 2 and 2, and B has none and none. The number of equal sides and the number of equal angles always match. Answer: A is equilateral (3 equal sides, 3 equal angles), B is scalene (no equal sides, no equal angles), C is isosceles (2 equal sides, 2 equal angles)

steps: Each piece is a triangle with 1 right angle and 3 different sides: a shortest side, a middle side and a longest side. The longest side is twice the shortest side.
Join 2 pieces side to side. They can meet along their shortest sides, their middle sides or their longest sides, and the second piece can be flipped over or turned half way round.
Along the middle sides, with one piece flipped over: a triangle with all 3 sides equal.
Along the shortest sides, with one piece flipped over: a wider triangle with 2 equal sides.
Along the longest sides, with one piece flipped over: a kite. With one piece turned half way round: a rectangle.
Along the middle sides or along the shortest sides, with one piece turned half way round: 2 different parallelograms that are not rectangles.
Check: 2 triangles and 4 four-sided shapes make 2 + 4 = 6 shapes, and each one has 3 or 4 sides.

steps: Take an isosceles triangle, for example the wider one made from 2 pieces. Its 2 equal sides meet at the top corner.
Fold it in half through the top corner, so that the 2 equal sides lie on each other. The fold is the line where the 2 pieces were joined.
The two halves match exactly. The two corners at the ends of the third side land on each other.
So the two angles at the ends of the third side are equal.
Check: fold the triangle with 3 equal sides in the same way. The halves match again, so equal sides go with equal angles.
content.answer: The two halves match when folded, so the two angles at the ends of the third side are equal. Each isosceles triangle has 2 equal angles.

content.book_number: Triangles from the Rhombus: an equilateral triangle
content.question: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal (equilateral triangle)?
steps: We want a triangle with 3 sides of the same length.
Join 2 pieces along their middle sides, with one piece flipped over.
The longest sides of the 2 pieces become 2 sides of the new triangle. They are equal.
The 2 shortest sides of the pieces lie in one straight line and make the third side. The shortest side is half the longest side, so 2 shortest sides are as long as 1 longest side.
So all 3 sides are equal: an equilateral triangle.
Check: measure the 3 sides with a ruler. They are the same.
content.answer: Yes. Join 2 pieces along their middle sides, with one piece flipped over. All 3 sides are equal, so it is an equilateral triangle.

content.question: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal?
steps: One piece is already a triangle. Its 3 sides are a shortest side, a middle side and a longest side, and they are all different.
So a single piece is a triangle with all 3 sides unequal.

Bigger ones are possible too. Join the wider triangle (2 pieces) and 1 more piece, longest side against one of the 2 equal sides, and flip the piece until the outside has only 3 sides. The 3 sides are all different.
A triangle with all 3 sides unequal is called a scalene triangle.
Check: a single piece has 3 different sides, so the answer is yes.
content.answer: Yes. A single piece has 3 different sides, and 3 pieces can also make a bigger triangle with 3 different sides. It is a scalene triangle.

media.teaching_notes: 1. We want a triangle with 3 sides of the same length. 2. Join 2 pieces along their middle sides, with one piece flipped over. 3. The longest sides of the 2 pieces become 2 sides of the new triangle. They are equal. 4. The 2 shortest sides of the pieces lie in one straight line and make the third side. The shortest side is half the longest side, so 2 shortest sides are as long as 1 longest side. 5. So all 3 sides are equal: an equilateral triangle. 6. Check: measure the 3 sides with a ruler. They are the same. Answer: Yes. Join 2 pieces along their middle sides, with one piece flipped over. All 3 sides are equal, so it is an equilateral triangle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: one four-sided shape has sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm and 3 cm, going round in that order. Another has sides 5 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm in that order. Both have two 5 cm sides and two 3 cm sides. Which one is a kite?
2. Adjacent sides are sides that meet at a corner. Opposite sides are across from each other.
3. In the first shape the two 5 cm sides meet at a corner, and the two 3 cm sides meet at a corner. Side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4, so it is a kite.
4. In the second shape the two 5 cm sides are across from each other, and so are the two 3 cm sides. The opposite sides are equal, so it is a parallelogram, not a kite.
5. Both shapes have the same side lengths. Only the order of the sides round the shape tells them apart.
6. Rule: in a kite the equal sides are adjacent (next to each other): side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4.

content.text:
Worked example: A four-sided shape has sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm and 3 cm going round in that order. Is it a kite? Then check a shape whose sides going round are 5 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm.
1. Name the sides in order: side 1 is 5 cm, side 2 is 5 cm, side 3 is 3 cm and side 4 is 3 cm.
2. Side 1 and side 2 are next to each other and both are 5 cm, so side 1 = side 2. They are adjacent sides.
3. Side 3 and side 4 are next to each other and both are 3 cm, so side 3 = side 4.
4. Two pairs of adjacent sides are equal, so the shape is a kite.
5. Now the second shape: 5 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm. Side 1 and side 3 are both 5 cm, but they are opposite sides, not next to each other.
6. Side 2 and side 4 are both 3 cm and also opposite. Equal opposite sides make a parallelogram, so this shape is not a kite.
7. Check: both shapes have two 5 cm sides and two 3 cm sides. Only the order round the shape decides.
Answer: The first shape is a kite, because its equal sides are next to each other (side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4). The second shape has equal opposite sides, so it is a parallelogram, not a kite

content.text:
Quadrilaterals whose opposite sides are equal are called parallelograms.
In parallelogram A, opposite angles are equal.
In parallelogram B, all angles are equal and are right angles. Such a parallelogram is called a rectangle.
A rectangle is a special type of parallelogram.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a four-sided shape has sides 8 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm going round. Is it a parallelogram? Is it a rectangle?
2. Look at the opposite sides: 8 cm and 8 cm, and 5 cm and 5 cm. Opposite sides are equal, so it is a parallelogram.
3. A parallelogram also has equal opposite angles. Now look at the angles. If all 4 angles are right angles, the parallelogram is a rectangle.
4. A slanted shape can have the same sides, 8 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm, and no right angle. It is a parallelogram that is not a rectangle.
5. So the sides alone do not tell us if a shape is a rectangle. We also need the angles.
6. Rule: a four-sided shape with equal opposite sides is a parallelogram; a parallelogram with 4 right angles is a rectangle, so a rectangle is a special parallelogram.

Worked example: A four-sided shape has sides 8 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm going round. What is it called? What more do we need to know to call it a rectangle?
1. Look at the opposite sides: the first and third sides are 8 cm and 8 cm, and the second and fourth sides are 5 cm and 5 cm.
2. Opposite sides are equal, so the shape is a parallelogram.
3. In a parallelogram the opposite angles are equal.
4. Now look at the angles. If all 4 angles are right angles, the parallelogram is a rectangle.
5. A slanted shape with the same sides 8 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm has no right angle. It is a parallelogram that is not a rectangle.
6. Check: every rectangle is a parallelogram, but a parallelogram is a rectangle only when its angles are right angles.
Answer: It is a parallelogram, because its opposite sides are equal. It is a rectangle only if all 4 angles are right angles; a slanted shape with the same sides is not a rectangle

media.title: Rhombus Pieces

tool_config.title: Rhombus Pieces
tool_config.idea: Join 2, 3 and 4 triangular pieces of the rhombus whole side to whole side, count the sides round the outside of the shape made, and name it. A joined side hides inside and sides in one straight line make one longer side, so each new piece adds at most 1 side. This tool joins pieces and counts sides; it does not measure given triangles.
tool_config.screen: The craft table seen from above, a warm wooden table drawn as a polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. In the middle lie the 4 triangular pieces of a rhombus, drawn large in blue, with a faint rhombus outline in the corner of the table that shows where they fit together. The pieces are the largest things on screen. Every piece is a triangle with 1 right angle, marked with a small square, and 3 different sides. To the right is a tracing sheet, a sheet of paper where the shape made is drawn as an outline with its outside edges thick. Under the table is a gallery strip with room for 6 small cards, where traced shapes are kept. Controls: drag a piece to move it; Turn turns the chosen piece one step at a time so that its sides line up with the other pieces; Flip flips the chosen piece over. A piece snaps whole side to whole side when one of its sides is brought near a side of the same length on another piece, with a soft click, and the joined sides turn into a dashed line inside the shape. Trace saves the shape to the tracing sheet and the gallery. Count lights each outside edge in orange one after the other while the side counter counts up. Name opens a label card with the names triangle, kite, parallelogram, rectangle, pentagon and hexagon to pick from. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Hint, Retry (separates the last piece), Reset (returns the 4 pieces to the rhombus), Undo, Back and Next are in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number of pieces used (1 to 4), the live side counter for the outside of the shape (for example Sides: 4), the name label, the number of shapes in the gallery, and the card number out of 7. On the last card the six shape names each get Yes and No buttons.

challenges: Card 1: join 2 pieces along their longest sides, with one piece flipped over. Trace it and count its sides. Answer: a kite with 4 sides. Side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4, so the equal sides are adjacent.

Card 2: join 2 pieces along their middle sides, with one piece turned half way round. Trace it and count its sides. Answer: a parallelogram with 4 sides. Its opposite sides are equal and none of its corners is a right angle, so it is not a rectangle.
Card 3: join 2 pieces along their longest sides, with one piece turned half way round. Trace it and count its sides. Answer: a rectangle with 4 sides and 4 right angles. Its opposite sides are equal.

Card 4: join 2 pieces along their middle sides, with one piece flipped over. Count the sides. Answer: 3 sides, not 4. The 2 shortest sides lie in one straight line and make one side. All 3 sides are equal: it is a triangle.

Card 5: use 3 pieces. Take the triangle from card 4 and join 1 more piece, its longest side against a side of the triangle. How many sides does the shape have? Answer: 4 sides, because 3 − 1 + 2 = 4: the joined side hides inside and the new piece adds 2 sides.

Challenge: 'Using 3 triangular pieces of the rhombus, try creating a (a) 3-sided shape, (b) 4-sided shape, and (c) 5-sided shape.' Build each one, trace it and read its sides. Answer: all three can be made. (a): join the wider triangle (2 pieces joined along their shortest sides) and 1 more piece, its longest side against one of the 2 equal sides, and flip the piece until the outside has 3 sides. (b): join the triangle with 3 equal sides and 1 more piece along a longest side, and the outside has 4 sides. (c): join 2 pieces along their shortest sides with one turned half way round, put the third piece with its longest side against one of the 2 long sides, and flip it until the outside has 5 sides. In all, 3 pieces make 13 different shapes, so your shapes may differ.

Challenge: 'Which of these shapes can be made with all 4 pieces? Try and find out. (a) Square (b) Rectangle (c) Triangle (d) Pentagon (5-sided) (e) Hexagon (6-sided) (f) Octagon (8-sided)' Try each one, then press Yes or No for each name. Answer: a rectangle, a triangle, a pentagon and a hexagon can be made. A square and an octagon cannot: each piece adds at most 1 side, so 4 pieces make at most 3 + 3 = 6 sides, and no four-sided shape made of 4 pieces has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.
feedback: When 2 sides touch whole side to whole side the pieces snap with a soft click, and the joined sides turn into a dashed line inside the shape. The tool says: Two sides are joined inside, so the outside has 4 sides.
Count lights each outside edge in orange one by one and the side counter counts up. Sides that line up in one straight line count as one side.
A piece brought near a side of a different length does not snap and wobbles gently with the note: These sides are not the same length. Try another side or turn the piece.
A name that does not fit the shape shows a soft amber note with a clue about sides or angles, for example: Are the equal sides next to each other or opposite each other?

On the book's cards the tool says what the shape has, for example: Your shape uses 3 pieces and has 5 sides. On the last card a Yes for a shape that has not been traced from all 4 pieces gets the note: Show it with all 4 pieces first. A wrong answer shows a soft amber note and never a red cross.

media.description: Concept video: Explain kites: adjacent sides equal, with a kite and a parallelogram of the same sides to compare. It works this example: A four-sided shape has sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm and 3 cm going round in that order. Is it a kite? Then check a shape whose sides going round are 5 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: one four-sided shape has sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm and 3 cm, going round in that order. Another has sides 5 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm in that order. Both have two 5 cm sides and two 3 cm sides. Which one is a kite? Adjacent sides are sides that meet at a corner. Opposite sides are across from each other. In the first shape the two 5 cm sides meet at a corner, and the two 3 cm sides meet at a corner. Side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4, so it is a kite. In the second shape the two 5 cm sides are across from each other, and so are the two 3 cm sides. The opposite sides are equal, so it is a parallelogram, not a kite. Both shapes have the same side lengths. Only the order of the sides round the shape tells them apart. Rule: in a kite the equal sides are adjacent (next to each other): side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4. 1. Name the sides in order: side 1 is 5 cm, side 2 is 5 cm, side 3 is 3 cm and side 4 is 3 cm. 2. Side 1 and side 2 are next to each other and both are 5 cm, so side 1 = side 2. They are adjacent sides. 3. Side 3 and side 4 are next to each other and both are 3 cm, so side 3 = side 4. 4. Two pairs of adjacent sides are equal, so the shape is a kite. 5. Now the second shape: 5 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm. Side 1 and side 3 are both 5 cm, but they are opposite sides, not next to each other. 6. Side 2 and side 4 are both 3 cm and also opposite. Equal opposite sides make a parallelogram, so this shape is not a kite. 7. Check: both shapes have two 5 cm sides and two 3 cm sides. Only the order round the shape decides. Answer: The first shape is a kite, because its equal sides are next to each other (side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4). The second shape has equal opposite sides, so it is a parallelogram, not a kite

media.description: Concept video: Explain parallelograms (opposite sides equal) and rectangles as special parallelograms with right angles. media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a four-sided shape has sides 8 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm going round. Is it a parallelogram? Is it a rectangle? Look at the opposite sides: 8 cm and 8 cm, and 5 cm and 5 cm. Opposite sides are equal, so it is a parallelogram. A parallelogram also has equal opposite angles. Now look at the angles. If all 4 angles are right angles, the parallelogram is a rectangle. A slanted shape can have the same sides, 8 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm, and no right angle. It is a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. So the sides alone do not tell us if a shape is a rectangle. We also need the angles. Rule: a four-sided shape with equal opposite sides is a parallelogram; a parallelogram with 4 right angles is a rectangle, so a rectangle is a special parallelogram. 1. Look at the opposite sides: the first and third sides are 8 cm and 8 cm, and the second and fourth sides are 5 cm and 5 cm. 2. Opposite sides are equal, so the shape is a parallelogram. 3. In a parallelogram the opposite angles are equal. 4. Now look at the angles. If all 4 angles are right angles, the parallelogram is a rectangle. 5. A slanted shape with the same sides 8 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm has no right angle. It is a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. 6. Check: every rectangle is a parallelogram, but a parallelogram is a rectangle only when its angles are right angles. Answer: It is a parallelogram, because its opposite sides are equal. It is a rectangle only if all 4 angles are right angles; a slanted shape with the same sides is not a rectangle

content.question: How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make?
steps: Join 2 pieces side to side. The joined side hides inside, so 2 pieces with 3 sides each give 3 + 3 − 2 = 4 sides outside, unless two sides line up in a straight line.
Join along the longest sides, with one piece flipped over: a kite.
Join along the longest sides, with one piece turned half way round: a rectangle.
Join along the middle sides, with one piece turned half way round: a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. Join along the shortest sides, with one piece turned half way round: another one.
That is 4 different four-sided shapes: a kite, a rectangle and 2 parallelograms. Sliding a piece along a joined side makes even more, so there are at least 4.
Check: each of the 4 shapes has 4 sides, counted round the outside.
content.answer: Sample answer: at least 4: a kite, a rectangle and 2 parallelograms that are not rectangles. Your answer may differ.

steps: Each piece has 3 sides, so 3 pieces have 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 sides. Joining 3 pieces takes 2 joins, and 4 of the 9 sides hide inside, so the outside has at most 9 − 4 = 5 sides. Sides that line up in a straight line make one longer side, so a shape can have fewer.

(a): 3-sided shape. Join the wider triangle (2 pieces joined along their shortest sides) and 1 more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against one of the 2 equal sides of the wider triangle. Flip the piece until the outside has 3 sides. It is a big triangle with 3 different sides.

(b): 4-sided shape. Join the triangle with 3 equal sides (2 pieces joined along their middle sides) and 1 more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against a side of the triangle. The outside has 4 sides.

(c): 5-sided shape. Join 2 pieces along their shortest sides, with one turned half way round, to make a slanted shape. Put the third piece with its longest side against one of the 2 long sides, and flip it until the outside has 5 sides.
Check: count the sides round the outside of each shape: 3, 4 and 5. In all, 3 pieces make 13 different shapes: 2 with 3 sides, 5 with 4 sides and 6 with 5 sides.

steps: Each new piece joined along a whole side covers 1 side and adds 2 new sides, so it adds at most 1 side.
A piece has 3 sides, and the other 3 pieces add at most 3 more. So 4 pieces make a shape with at most 3 + 3 = 6 sides.

(a): no square. A square needs 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. The shape with 4 equal sides that 4 pieces make is the rhombus, which has no right angle, and the rectangles have 2 different side lengths.
(b): rectangle, yes. Make a rectangle from 2 pieces (longest sides together, one piece turned half way round), make a second one the same, and join the 2 rectangles along sides of the same length.

(c): triangle, yes. Join the triangle with 3 equal sides (2 pieces) and the wider triangle (2 pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has only 3 sides. They make a big triangle.
(d): pentagon, yes. Join a kite (2 pieces) and a rectangle (2 pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has 5 sides.
(e): hexagon, yes. Join 2 kites along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has 6 sides.
(f): no octagon. A shape made of 4 pieces has at most 6 sides, and an octagon has 8.
Check: yes for the rectangle, triangle, pentagon and hexagon, and no for the square and the octagon.

1. Each new piece joined along a whole side covers $1$ side and adds $2$ new sides, so it adds at most $1$ side.
2. A piece has $3$ sides, and the other $3$ pieces add at most $3$ more. So $4$ pieces make a shape with at most $3 + 3 = 6$ sides.
[Image: Shapes from the Rhombus: Ans6: solution]
3. $(a)$: no square. A square needs $4$ equal sides and $4$ right angles. The shape with $4$ equal sides that $4$ pieces make is the rhombus, which has no right angle, and the rectangles have $2$ different side lengths.
4. $(b)$: rectangle, yes. Make a rectangle from $2$ pieces (longest sides together, one piece turned half way round), make a second one the same, and join the $2$ rectangles along sides of the same length.
5. $(c)$: triangle, yes. Join the triangle with $3$ equal sides ($2$ pieces) and the wider triangle ($2$ pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has only $3$ sides. They make a big triangle.
6. $(d)$: pentagon, yes. Join a kite ($2$ pieces) and a rectangle ($2$ pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has $5$ sides.
7. $(e)$: hexagon, yes. Join $2$ kites along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has $6$ sides.
8. $(f)$: no octagon. A shape made of $4$ pieces has at most $6$ sides, and an octagon has $8$.
9. Check: yes for the rectangle, triangle, pentagon and hexagon, and no for the square and the octagon.
Answer: A rectangle, a triangle, a pentagon and a hexagon can be made. A square and an octagon cannot.

media.title: Shapes from the Rhombus: three triangles
media.context: Shapes and Patterns. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Question video: Now, use 3 triangles from the rhombus to form shapes. How many sides do each one of them have? Using 3 triangular pieces of the rhombus, try creating: (a): a 3-sided shape; (b): a 4-sided shape; (c): a 5-sided shape.
media.teaching_notes: 1. Each piece has 3 sides, so 3 pieces have 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 sides. Joining 3 pieces takes 2 joins, and 4 of the 9 sides hide inside, so the outside has at most 9 − 4 = 5 sides. Sides that line up in a straight line make one longer side, so a shape can have fewer. 2. (a): 3-sided shape. Join the wider triangle (2 pieces joined along their shortest sides) and 1 more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against one of the 2 equal sides of the wider triangle. Flip the piece until the outside has 3 sides. It is a big triangle with 3 different sides. 3. (b): 4-sided shape. Join the triangle with 3 equal sides (2 pieces joined along their middle sides) and 1 more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against a side of the triangle. The outside has 4 sides. 4. (c): 5-sided shape. Join 2 pieces along their shortest sides, with one turned half way round, to make a slanted shape. Put the third piece with its longest side against one of the 2 long sides, and flip it until the outside has 5 sides. 5. Check: count the sides round the outside of each shape: 3, 4 and 5. In all, 3 pieces make 13 different shapes: 2 with 3 sides, 5 with 4 sides and 6 with 5 sides. Answer: Sample answer: yes. (a): a big triangle with 3 different sides. (b): the triangle with 3 equal sides and 1 more piece, 4 sides. (c): a slanted shape and 1 more piece, 5 sides. Your answer may differ.

content.book_number: Kites: make a kite by folding
content.question: Make your own kite shape. (a): Start with a square piece of paper. (b): Take one corner of the paper and fold it towards the opposite corner, creating a sharp crease along the diagonal. (c): Open and fold the corner A inwards, aligning the edge with the crease you just made. (d): Repeat on the other side, folding the other corner B inwards to align with the crease at the centre. You have a kite shape! What shapes do you see in the kite?

content.book_number: Kites: make a kite by folding
content.question: Make your own kite shape. (a): Start with a square piece of paper. (b): Take one corner of the paper and fold it towards the opposite corner, creating a sharp crease along the diagonal. (c): Open and fold the corner A inwards, aligning the edge with the crease you just made. (d): Repeat on the other side, folding the other corner B inwards to align with the crease at the centre. You have a kite shape! What shapes do you see in the kite?
steps: Fold the corner A onto the corner across from it, which is B, and open it again. The crease runs along the other diagonal of the square.
Fold the corner A inwards so that one edge of the paper lies along the crease. The folded part is a triangle.
Fold the corner B inwards in the same way, from the same end of the crease, so that its edge lies along the crease too. This folded part is also a triangle.
The paper now has the shape of a kite: 2 pairs of adjacent sides are equal.
Look at the shapes: the 2 folded flaps are 2 triangles, and the paper under them shows 2 more triangles. The crease also cuts the kite into 2 triangles.
Check: 2 flaps and 2 triangles under them make 2 + 2 = 4 triangles.
content.answer: Sample answer: triangles. The kite is made of 4 triangles: the 2 folded flaps and 2 more under them. It also splits along the crease into 2 triangles. Your answer may differ.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a tangram set has 7 pieces. If you sort them by the number of sides, how many pieces have 3 sides and how many have 4 sides?
2. Pieces with 3 sides are triangles. There are 5 of them, in three sizes: 2 small, 1 medium and 2 large.
3. Pieces with 4 sides are the square and the parallelogram. That makes 5 + 2 = 7 pieces.
4. Look at the corners. Every triangle has 1 right angle and 2 equal angles. The square has 4 right angles and 4 equal sides. The parallelogram has no right angle.
5. Rule: sort the pieces by their sides first, 5 triangles and 2 four-sided pieces, then compare their sizes, sides and angles.
