content.text:
Worked example: A tangram has 7 pieces: 2 small triangles, 1 medium triangle, 2 large triangles, a square and a parallelogram. Sort them by the number of sides, and say what is special about the angles of each group.
1. Count the sides of each piece. A triangle has 3 sides. The square and the parallelogram have 4 sides each.
2. 3 sides: the 2 small triangles, the 1 medium triangle and the 2 large triangles. That is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 triangles.
3. 4 sides: the square and the parallelogram. That is 2 pieces.
4. Together the two groups hold 5 + 2 = 7 pieces.
5. Each of the 5 triangles has 1 right angle and 2 equal angles.
6. The square has 4 right angles and 4 equal sides. The parallelogram has no right angle.
7. Check: each of the 7 pieces is in exactly one group.
Answer: 3 sides: 5 triangles (2 small, 1 medium, 2 large). 4 sides: the square and the parallelogram. 5 + 2 = 7 pieces. Every triangle has a right angle and 2 equal angles

tool_config.title: Tangram Maker
tool_config.idea: Name the seven tangram pieces and make target shapes from some or all of them: sort the pieces by their number of sides, make a square from 2 small triangles, and fill outlines by turning and flipping pieces, finding that a shape can often be made in more than one way.
tool_config.screen: A wooden tangram tray on the craft table, drawn as a polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The 7 pieces lie in the tray as flat coloured pieces, large and clear: 2 large triangles, 1 medium triangle, 2 small triangles, a square and a parallelogram. An outline of the shape to make sits in the middle of the table and is the largest thing on screen; the pieces are dragged onto it. Above the table, 4 outline cards sit in a row: a slanted parallelogram, a rectangle twice as long as it is tall, a triangle with a right angle at the top, and a four-sided shape with a short top and a long bottom. Tap a card to bring its outline to the middle. Controls: drag a piece to move it; Turn turns the chosen piece one step at a time; Flip flips the chosen piece over; a piece snaps to a side or a corner of the outline when it is close, with a soft click; tap a piece to show its name label (for example large triangle); Check looks at the outline. Two sorting trays labelled 3 sides and 4 sides appear on the sorting card. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Hint, Retry (clears the outline), Reset (returns all the pieces to the tray), Undo, Back and Next are in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the name label of the chosen piece, the number of pieces in the outline (for example pieces in the outline: 3), a message line that says what Check found, and the card number out of 5.
student_does: Look at the 7 pieces from the video, the 5 triangles and the 2 four-sided pieces. Tap one piece of each kind and say how many sides it has, then press Next.
Tap each piece to read its name label, make a square from 2 small triangles, and fill the triangle outline in 2 different ways.
Use some or all of the pieces to make the 4 shapes from your maths book, and find a way to fill each outline.
challenges: Card 1: sort the 7 pieces into the trays 3 sides and 4 sides, and tap each piece to read its name. Answer: 3 sides: 2 large triangles, 1 medium triangle and 2 small triangles (5 pieces). 4 sides: the square and the parallelogram (2 pieces). 5 + 2 = 7 pieces.
Card 2: make a square from 2 small triangles. Answer: join the 2 small triangles along their longest sides. They make a square the same size as the tangram square.
Card 3: fill the triangle outline (a right angle at the top) with 1 piece. Answer: the medium triangle fills it, with its longest side at the bottom.

Card 4: clear the triangle outline and fill it again with 2 pieces. Answer: the 2 small triangles fill it, side by side with their right angles together at the middle of the bottom. A shape can be made in more than one way.

Challenge: 'Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it.' Fill all 4 outlines. Answer: one way for each, and yours may differ. The rectangle: the medium triangle in the middle with its longest side at the bottom and a small triangle in the gap on each side. The slanted parallelogram: the medium triangle on the left and the 2 small triangles together on the right. The triangle: the medium triangle. The four-sided shape with a short top and a long bottom: the parallelogram on the left and the medium triangle on the right, with the longest side of the medium triangle at the bottom. The rectangle can also be made from the square and the 2 small triangles.
feedback: A piece brought close to a side or a corner of the outline snaps in with a soft click. Pieces that overlap each other or stick out of the outline glow soft amber with the note: These pieces overlap. Move one piece.

Check says what it sees. A full outline gets: The outline is full with no gap and no overlap. A gap glows amber with a clue, for example: A gap is left near the top corner. Which piece has a corner that fits it?

After an outline is filled the tool says: These pieces fit the shape: more than one way is allowed. It then invites the student to press Retry and fill the same outline with a different set of pieces.

On the sorting card a piece dropped in the wrong tray slides back with the clue: Count the sides of this piece. A name label that does not fit the piece shows the amber note: Look at the size and at the number of sides.
A wrong answer shows a soft amber note and never a red cross; the tool names the piece it expected only after the second try.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 pieces are sorted and named, a square is made from 2 small triangles, the triangle outline is filled in 2 different ways, and all 4 outlines from the book are filled.

hint_ladder.text: Look at the biggest corner of the outline: which piece has a corner like it?
Place the largest piece that fits first, then fill the gaps that are left with smaller pieces. Turn or flip a piece if it does not fit.
For the rectangle, lay the longest side of the medium triangle along the bottom. A small triangle fits the gap on each side.
The tool places one piece in the outline for you, and then a similar card follows.

media.description: Concept video: Show the seven tangram pieces sorted by number of sides, with their sides and angles. It works this example: A tangram has 7 pieces: 2 small triangles, 1 medium triangle, 2 large triangles, a square and a parallelogram. Sort them by the number of sides, and say what is special about the angles of each group.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a tangram set has 7 pieces. If you sort them by the number of sides, how many pieces have 3 sides and how many have 4 sides? Pieces with 3 sides are triangles. There are 5 of them, in three sizes: 2 small, 1 medium and 2 large. Pieces with 4 sides are the square and the parallelogram. That makes 5 + 2 = 7 pieces. Look at the corners. Every triangle has 1 right angle and 2 equal angles. The square has 4 right angles and 4 equal sides. The parallelogram has no right angle. Rule: sort the pieces by their sides first, 5 triangles and 2 four-sided pieces, then compare their sizes, sides and angles. 1. Count the sides of each piece. A triangle has 3 sides. The square and the parallelogram have 4 sides each. 2. 3 sides: the 2 small triangles, the 1 medium triangle and the 2 large triangles. That is 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 triangles. 3. 4 sides: the square and the parallelogram. That is 2 pieces. 4. Together the two groups hold 5 + 2 = 7 pieces. 5. Each of the 5 triangles has 1 right angle and 2 equal angles. 6. The square has 4 right angles and 4 equal sides. The parallelogram has no right angle. 7. Check: each of the 7 pieces is in exactly one group. Answer: 3 sides: 5 triangles (2 small, 1 medium, 2 large). 4 sides: the square and the parallelogram. 5 + 2 = 7 pieces. Every triangle has a right angle and 2 equal angles

content.book_number: Tangram: name the pieces
content.question: Look at the tangram set. Cut out all the shapes. Name them.
steps: Count the sides of each piece and compare the sizes.
5 pieces have 3 sides, so they are triangles. The 2 biggest are the large triangles, the 2 smallest are the small triangles, and the one in between is the medium triangle.
2 pieces have 4 sides. One has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles: the square. The other is slanted with equal opposite sides: the parallelogram.
Check: 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7 pieces.
content.answer: 2 large triangles, 1 medium triangle, 2 small triangles, 1 square and 1 parallelogram.

4. Check: $2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7$ pieces.
Answer: $2$ large triangles, $1$ medium triangle, $2$ small triangles, $1$ square and $1$ parallelogram.

The 5 triangles have the same shape in 3 sizes: the 2 small triangles are the same size, the 2 large triangles are the same size, and the medium triangle is in between.
Look at what is different. The sizes are different, and the square and the parallelogram have 4 sides while the triangles have 3.
Check: 5 triangles and 2 four-sided pieces make 5 + 2 = 7 pieces.
content.answer: Same: all have straight sides, and the 5 triangles have the same shape. Different: the sizes differ, and the square and parallelogram have 4 sides, not 3.

Look at the square. All 4 angles are right angles, so all 4 are equal.

Check: fold a triangle in half through its right angle. The other 2 corners land on each other, so those 2 angles are equal.

content.book_number: Tangram: make the shapes
content.question: Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it.
steps: Use some or all of the 7 pieces. The pieces must not overlap, and they must fill the outline with no gap.
Rectangle: put the medium triangle in the middle with its longest side at the bottom. Put a small triangle in the gap on each side. The 3 pieces fill the rectangle.

Slanted parallelogram: put the medium triangle on the left. Put the 2 small triangles together on the right, so that they make a second triangle the size of the medium one. The 2 triangles side by side make the slanted shape.
Triangle: the medium triangle fills it, with its longest side at the bottom. The 2 small triangles also fill it, side by side with their right angles together at the middle of the bottom.
Four-sided shape with a short top and a long bottom: put the parallelogram on the left and the medium triangle on the right, with the longest side of the medium triangle at the bottom.
More than one way: the rectangle can also be made from the square and the 2 small triangles, and the parallelogram from the square with a small triangle on each side.
Check: each outline is filled with no gap and no overlap.
content.answer: Sample answer: rectangle and parallelogram: medium triangle and 2 small triangles. Triangle: medium triangle. Last shape: parallelogram and medium triangle. Your answer may differ.

7. Check: each outline is filled with no gap and no overlap.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a shape has opposite sides equal. Is it a square, a rectangle, a rhombus or a parallelogram?
2. Ask two questions about a four-sided shape. Are all four sides equal? Are all four angles right angles?
3. All sides equal and all angles right angles: a square. Opposite sides equal and all angles right angles: a rectangle.
4. All sides equal and the angles are not right angles: a rhombus. Opposite sides equal, the sides next to each other different and no right angles: a parallelogram.
5. Opposite sides equal is true of all four shapes. So that one statement fits all four shapes, and a rectangle is a special parallelogram.
6. Rule: check the sides, then the angles. One statement can fit more than one shape.

content.text:
Worked example: Four shapes are described. X: all sides 6 cm and all angles right angles. Y: sides 9 cm, 4 cm, 9 cm, 4 cm and all angles right angles. Z: all sides 7 cm and the angles are not right angles. W: sides 8 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm, 5 cm in order and the angles are not right angles. Name each shape. Which of them have opposite sides equal?
1. X: all four sides are equal (6 cm) and all four angles are right angles: a square.
2. Y: the sides are not all equal (9 cm and 4 cm), but opposite sides are equal and all angles are right angles: a rectangle.
3. Z: all four sides are equal (7 cm) and the angles are not right angles: a rhombus.
4. W: opposite sides are equal (8 cm and 8 cm, 5 cm and 5 cm), the sides are not all equal and the angles are not right angles: a parallelogram.
5. Now test the statement opposite sides are equal: X yes, Y yes, Z yes, W yes. All four shapes have it.
6. Check: a statement about opposite sides alone does not tell the four shapes apart, so it fits more than one shape. Adding all angles are right angles keeps only X and Y.
Answer: X is a square, Y is a rectangle, Z is a rhombus and W is a parallelogram. All four have opposite sides equal, so that one statement fits all four

tool_config.title: Shape Detective
tool_config.idea: Drag the corners of one four-sided shape and switch two locks to see when it is a square, a rectangle, a rhombus or a parallelogram, then test seven statements about sides and angles and see that one statement can fit more than one shape.
tool_config.screen: The detective's board on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3-D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A pinboard in the middle holds one four-sided shape on a dot grid, and it is the largest thing on screen. The shape has four round corner handles that can be dragged. Its four sides show their lengths in centimetres next to them (practice values), and every corner that is a right angle carries a small square mark. To the left of the board are two locks: a Sides lock with three positions, Off, Opposite sides equal and All sides equal, and an Angles lock with two positions, Off and Right angles. A name plate above the shape reads Four-sided shape, Parallelogram, Rhombus, Rectangle or Square, whichever fits the shape now. Along the bottom lies a shelf of seven statement cards numbered 1 to 7 with the book's wording, and on the right are four shape cards: Square, Rectangle, Rhombus and Parallelogram. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a corner handle (the locks decide what the other corners do, so the sides or angles stay as set); switch each lock; drag a statement card onto the shape to test it, or onto a shape card to match it; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the last match), Reset (clears all matches and unlocks the shape), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the four side lengths, the right angle marks, the name plate, a tester light on each statement card that shows fits in green or look again in soft amber with the reason, and a match tally that counts how many statements are matched to each shape (for example Rhombus: 3).
student_does: Look at the four shapes from the video on the board. X has all sides 6 cm and all angles right angles. Y has sides 9 cm and 4 cm and all angles right angles. Z has all sides 7 cm and no right angles. W has sides 8 cm and 5 cm and no right angles. Name each shape and say what is the same in all four.

Switch the locks one at a time and drag a corner to make a square, a rectangle, a rhombus and a parallelogram, reading the name plate each time. Then drag a statement card onto your shape and read whether it fits.
The book's own question with the seven statement cards and the four shape cards. Match the statements with appropriate shapes. Do some of them describe more than one shape?
challenges: Card 1: set the Sides lock to All sides equal and the Angles lock to Right angles, then drag a corner. What shape is it, and what happens to the sides when you drag? Answer: a square. The four sides grow or shrink together and stay equal, and the four angles stay right angles.

Card 2: set the Sides lock to Opposite sides equal and the Angles lock to Right angles, then drag a corner. Which shape is it? Answer: a rectangle. Opposite sides stay equal, the four angles stay right angles, and the sides next to each other can be different.

Card 3: set the Sides lock to All sides equal and the Angles lock to Off, then drag a corner until no angle is a right angle. Which shape is it? Answer: a rhombus. All four sides are equal and the angles are not right angles.

Card 4: set the Sides lock to Opposite sides equal and the Angles lock to Off, then drag a corner so that the sides next to each other are different and no angle is a right angle. Which shape is it? Answer: a parallelogram. Opposite sides are equal and the angles are not right angles.

Card 5: make each of your four shapes in turn and drag statement 6, 'My opposite angles are equal and so are my sides.', onto it. On which shapes does it fit? Answer: on all four, because each of them has opposite sides equal and opposite angles equal.

Challenge: 'Match the statements with appropriate shapes. Do some of them describe more than one shape?' The statements are 1: All my angles are right angles, but all my sides are not equal. 2: All my sides are equal, but all my angles are not. 3: My opposite angles are equal, but my sides do not make a right angle. 4: Two pairs of sides are equal, but they do not make a right angle. 5: All my sides make right angles with each other and are equal. 6: My opposite angles are equal and so are my sides. 7: My opposite angles are equal and my sides make right angles. The shapes are Square, Rectangle, Rhombus and Parallelogram. Answer: 1 Rectangle; 2 Rhombus; 3 Rhombus and Parallelogram; 4 Parallelogram and Rhombus; 5 Square; 6 all four shapes; 7 Square and Rectangle. Yes, statements 3, 4, 6 and 7 describe more than one shape.
feedback: A statement card dropped on a shape shows a green tester light when it fits and a soft amber light when it does not, with the reason, for example: Statement 7 fits the rectangle: its opposite angles are equal and its sides make right angles.
When a lock is set the shape keeps what the lock says while you drag. Under Opposite sides equal the other corners follow, so the opposite sides stay equal, and the name plate changes at once.
A rectangle also has opposite angles equal: statement 7 fits it too, so the tool says that one statement can fit more than one shape.
Statement 1 dropped on the square shows soft amber: all my angles are right angles is true for the square, but its sides are all equal, so all my sides are not equal does not fit.

A wrong match slides back with a clue such as: Check the sides first. Are all four equal? It never shows a red mark. A shape card that has a match gets a small green tick and the tally counts it, for example: Statement 3 fits 2 shapes.

media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a shape has opposite sides equal. Is it a square, a rectangle, a rhombus or a parallelogram? Ask two questions about a four-sided shape. Are all four sides equal? Are all four angles right angles? All sides equal and all angles right angles: a square. Opposite sides equal and all angles right angles: a rectangle. All sides equal and the angles are not right angles: a rhombus. Opposite sides equal, the sides next to each other different and no right angles: a parallelogram. Opposite sides equal is true of all four shapes. So that one statement fits all four shapes, and a rectangle is a special parallelogram. Rule: check the sides, then the angles. One statement can fit more than one shape. 1. X: all four sides are equal (6 cm) and all four angles are right angles: a square. 2. Y: the sides are not all equal (9 cm and 4 cm), but opposite sides are equal and all angles are right angles: a rectangle. 3. Z: all four sides are equal (7 cm) and the angles are not right angles: a rhombus. 4. W: opposite sides are equal (8 cm and 8 cm, 5 cm and 5 cm), the sides are not all equal and the angles are not right angles: a parallelogram. 5. Now test the statement opposite sides are equal: X yes, Y yes, Z yes, W yes. All four shapes have it. 6. Check: a statement about opposite sides alone does not tell the four shapes apart, so it fits more than one shape. Adding all angles are right angles keeps only X and Y. Answer: X is a square, Y is a rectangle, Z is a rhombus and W is a parallelogram. All four have opposite sides equal, so that one statement fits all four

content.text:
1. Predict first: draw two diameters of a circle and join their four ends. What shape do you get? Are its angles right angles?
2. A diameter is a line from one side of the circle to the other that passes through the centre. Every diameter of a circle has the same length, and the radius is half of it.
3. Two diameters cross at the centre. All four ends are the same distance from the centre.
4. Join the four ends in order and check. Opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles: a rectangle.
5. Turn one diameter and join again. The sides change, but the shape is still a rectangle.
6. If the two diameters cross at a right angle, all four sides are equal: a square, which is a special rectangle.
7. Rule: the four ends of two diameters always make a rectangle.

content.text:
Worked example: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. Draw two diameters and join their four ends. What is the radius? What shape is formed? What shape is formed when the two diameters cross at a right angle?
1. The diameter is 10 cm, so the radius is half of it: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
2. Draw one diameter and a second diameter. Both go through the centre, so both are 10 cm long.
3. Join the four ends in order. The shape has 4 sides: it is a quadrilateral.
4. Check the sides: opposite sides are equal.
5. Check the angles: all four are right angles. Opposite sides equal and four right angles: a rectangle.
6. Now turn the second diameter until it crosses the first one at a right angle. All four sides come out equal: a square. A square is a special rectangle.
7. Check: the four ends are all 5 cm from the centre and the two diameters are 10 cm each, so every pair of diameters gives a rectangle.
Answer: The radius is 5 cm. Two diameters joined at their ends make a rectangle. If they cross at a right angle it is a square, a special rectangle

content.text:
1. Predict first: a circle has 12 points numbered 1 to 12. You join 1 to 5, then 5 to 2, then 2 to 6, and keep going. Does the thread ever come back to 1?
2. Look for the move. 1 to 5 goes on by 4. 5 to 2 goes back by 3. 2 to 6 goes on by 4 again.
3. Keep the same moves: on by 4, back by 3, on by 4, back by 3. Each pair of moves goes on by 1 in all, so the thread starts a little further round each time.
4. When you pass 12, the numbers start again from 1. From 9, going on by 4 takes you to 10, 11, 12 and then 1.
5. The thread is back at 1 and the design is closed. Now count the lines.
6. Rule: find the move, repeat it until the thread is back at the start, then count the lines.

When you pass 12, the numbers start again from 1. From 9, going on by 4 takes you to 10, 11, 12 and then 1.
The thread is back at 1 and the design is closed. Now count the lines.
Rule: find the move, repeat it until the thread is back at the start, then count the lines.

content.text:
Worked example: A circle has 12 points numbered 1 to 12 round it. Join 1 to 5, 5 to 2, 2 to 6, 6 to 3, and so on until you reach 1 again. How many lines do you draw?
1. Find the move: 1 to 5 is on by 4, 5 to 2 is back by 3, 2 to 6 is on by 4.
2. Keep the same moves: on by 4, back by 3, on by 4, back by 3.
3. Write the points in order: 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 5, 9, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 9. From 9 go on by 4: 10, 11, 12, then 1. The thread is back at 1.
4. Count the lines: each line joins a point to the next one in the list. The list has 18 points with the last 1, so there are 18 − 1 = 17 lines.
5. Check: 8 pairs of moves (on by 4, back by 3) use 16 lines, and one last move on by 4 closes the design, so 8 × 2 + 1 = 17 lines.
Answer: 17 lines. The path is 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7, 4, 8, 5, 9, 6, 10, 7, 11, 8, 12, 9, 1

tool_config.title: Circle Stitcher
tool_config.idea: Draw two diameters of a circle, join their four ends and check the sides and the angles to see that the shape is always a rectangle, then thread the points of a circle by a repeating move to make a string design that closes when the thread is back at the start.
tool_config.screen: A compass board and a thread board on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3-D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Three tabs at the top of the table switch between the Compass board, the Thread board and the Circle design mat. On the Compass board a circle with a diameter of 10 cm and its centre marked is the largest thing on screen. Two diameters pass through the centre and each end of each diameter is a round handle, so four points sit on the circle. Compass board controls: drag a handle to turn its diameter; a Join button that joins the four ends in order with a dotted line; a turn slider that turns the second diameter slowly all the way round; a Right angle snap that puts the second diameter at a right angle to the first. Compass board read-outs: the four side lengths in centimetres, a small square mark on every angle that is a right angle, and a name plate that reads Rectangle or Square. On the Thread board there is a circle with 12 points numbered 1 to 12 (practice values) or a circle with 24 points numbered 1 to 24, as in your maths book, with a tray of four coloured threads: teal, amber, green and reddish purple. Thread board controls: tap one point and then another to pull a thread between them; tap a colour in the tray to change the thread; Undo takes off the last thread. Thread board read-outs: a Move read-out that names the last move, for example on by 10 or back by 9, the number of lines threaded, and a Closed light that turns green when the thread is back at the first point. On the Circle design mat there is a circle with a radius of 3 cm (practice values), its centre marked and two diameters at right angles, so four points sit on the circle. Circle design mat controls: a Compass opening handle that sets the radius of the circle to draw, and a Draw circle button that draws a circle with its centre on the point you tap; read-outs: the compass opening in centimetres and the number of circles drawn. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the last lines or the last circle), Reset (clears the board), Back and Next sit in the same places on every card.
student_does: Look at the 12-point circle from the video, where the thread goes 1, 5, 2, 6, 3, 7 and on. Say the move: on by how many, then back by how many?

On the Compass board draw two diameters, join the ends and read the sides and the angles, turn one diameter and look again, then make the diameters cross at a right angle. Then thread a 12-point circle by a move of your own and try the compass on the design mat.

The book's own questions. Is it possible to create a 4-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process? Then thread the 24 points: join points 1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, and so on till you reach back at 1.
challenges: Card 1: on the Compass board drag the handles to make two diameters and press Join. Read the sides and the angles. What shape is it? Answer: a rectangle. Opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles.

Card 2: turn the second diameter with the slider and watch the read-outs. What changes and what stays the same? Answer: the side lengths change, but the four angles stay right angles and the name plate stays Rectangle.
Card 3: press Right angle snap. What shape is it now? Answer: a square. All four sides are equal and all four angles are right angles. A square is a special rectangle.

Card 4 (practice values): on the Thread board with 12 points, join 1 to 4, 4 to 2, 2 to 5 and keep going until you are back at 1. What is the move, and how many lines did you thread? Answer: on by 3, then back by 2, and 19 lines.

Card 5 (practice values): on the Circle design mat set the compass opening to 3 cm, the radius of the circle, and draw a circle with its centre on one of the 4 points. What do you see? Answer: a new circle of the same size that passes through the centre of the first circle.

Challenge: 'Is it possible to create a 4-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process?' Turn the diameters into as many positions as you like before you answer. Answer: no. The shape is always a rectangle. When the two diameters cross at a right angle it is a square, which is a special rectangle.

Challenge: 'Look at the circle given below. It is marked with points 1 to 24. Join points 1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, and so on till you reach back at 1.' Answer: 29 lines. The thread goes on by 10, then back by 9, and it is back at 1 after 29 lines.
feedback: When the four ends are joined, the read-outs show the four sides and the four angles and the tool says, for example: Opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles: a rectangle.
When you turn a diameter the sides change and the tool says: The sides changed, the angles are still right angles, so it is still a rectangle.
When the diameters cross at a right angle the name plate says Square and the tool says: All four sides are equal now, a square is a special rectangle.

Each thread draws from one point to the next and the Move read-out names the move, for example: 1 to 11 is on by 10, 11 to 2 is back by 9. A tap on a point that does not follow the move gives a soft amber note such as: The move from 11 is back by 9, so look for point 2.

When the thread is back at the first point the Closed light turns green and the tool shows the number of lines, for example 29 lines. On the design mat the new circle is drawn with its centre on the point you tapped and the tool says: Same opening, same size.
tool_config.done_when: The student has joined two diameters and seen a rectangle, turned a diameter and seen a rectangle again, made a square, threaded a closed design on the 12-point circle, answered the book's two questions and threaded the 24 points back to point 1.

media.description: Concept video: Show that joining the ends of two diameters of a circle makes a rectangle, and a square when the diameters cross at a right angle. It works this example: A circle has a diameter of 10 cm. Draw two diameters and join their four ends. What is the radius? What shape is formed? What shape is formed when the two diameters cross at a right angle?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: draw two diameters of a circle and join their four ends. What shape do you get? Are its angles right angles? A diameter is a line from one side of the circle to the other that passes through the centre. Every diameter of a circle has the same length, and the radius is half of it. Two diameters cross at the centre. All four ends are the same distance from the centre. Join the four ends in order and check. Opposite sides are equal and all four angles are right angles: a rectangle. Turn one diameter and join again. The sides change, but the shape is still a rectangle. If the two diameters cross at a right angle, all four sides are equal: a square, which is a special rectangle. Rule: the four ends of two diameters always make a rectangle. 1. The diameter is 10 cm, so the radius is half of it: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm. 2. Draw one diameter and a second diameter. Both go through the centre, so both are 10 cm long. 3. Join the four ends in order. The shape has 4 sides: it is a quadrilateral. 4. Check the sides: opposite sides are equal. 5. Check the angles: all four are right angles. Opposite sides equal and four right angles: a rectangle. 6. Now turn the second diameter until it crosses the first one at a right angle. All four sides come out equal: a square. A square is a special rectangle. 7. Check: the four ends are all 5 cm from the centre and the two diameters are 10 cm each, so every pair of diameters gives a rectangle. Answer: The radius is 5 cm. Two diameters joined at their ends make a rectangle. If they cross at a right angle it is a square, a special rectangle

steps: Draw a circle with a compass. Say the radius is 4 cm, so the diameter is 4 × 2 = 8 cm. Mark the centre.
Draw one diameter through the centre and mark its two ends.

content.question: Is it possible to create a 4-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process?
steps: Every pair of diameters gives a rectangle: opposite sides equal and four right angles.
Turn one diameter all the way round the centre. The four ends always make a rectangle, and never a different 4-sided shape.
When the two diameters cross at a right angle, all four sides are equal: a square. A square is a special rectangle, so it is not a different shape.
Check: in every try the four angles were right angles, so the shape is a rectangle.
content.answer: No. The shape is always a rectangle. When the diameters cross at a right angle it is a square, which is a special rectangle.

content.book_number: Circle Designs: join the points
content.question: Look at the circle given below. It is marked with points 1 to 24. Join points 1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, and so on till you reach back at 1.
steps: Find the move: 1 to 11 goes on by 10. 11 to 2 goes back by 9. 2 to 12 goes on by 10 again.
From 15 go on by 10: 16, 17 and on to 24, then 1. The thread is back at 1.
Count the lines: 14 pairs of moves make 14 × 2 = 28 lines, and the last move on by 10 makes 1 more line, so 28 + 1 = 29.
Check: the list of points has 30 places with the last 1, so there are 30 − 1 = 29 lines.
content.answer: 29 lines. The thread goes on by 10, back by 9, and is back at 1 after 29 lines.

steps: Look at the picture: 5 circles of the same size, one in the middle and four round it.

Check: each of the 4 new circles passes through the centre of the middle circle, as in the picture.

concepts.concept_name: Faces of a Cube and Its Net

content.text:
1. Predict first: in one view of a cube the heart touches the sun and the leaf. In another view the moon touches the sun and the leaf. Which face is opposite the heart?
2. Faces that you see together in one view touch each other, so they are not opposite. Opposite faces are never seen together.
3. The heart touches the sun and the leaf. The moon also touches the sun and the leaf. The sun and the leaf touch each other along one edge, and the two faces at the two ends of that edge are opposite.
4. So the heart is opposite the moon.
5. A net is a cube cut open and laid flat: 6 squares joined by their sides. In a straight row of 3 squares, the first and the third fold up to opposite faces.
6. Rule: two faces that both touch the same two touching faces are opposite each other.

content.text:
Worked example: A cube has six faces: sun, moon, heart, leaf, star and a plain face. In View 1 the sun is on top, the heart is on the left and the leaf is on the right. In View 2 the sun is on top, the leaf is on the left and the moon is on the right. Which face is opposite the heart?
1. View 1: the heart touches the sun and the leaf.
2. View 2: the moon touches the sun and the leaf.
3. So the heart and the moon both touch the same two faces, the sun and the leaf.
4. The sun and the leaf touch each other along one edge. The two faces at the two ends of that edge are opposite each other, and they are the heart and the moon.
5. So the heart is opposite the moon.
6. Check: opposite faces are never seen together. The heart is in View 1 and the moon is in View 2, and they never appear in the same view.
Answer: The moon is opposite the heart

concepts.concept_name: Counting Small Cubes in a Big Cube

content.text:
1. Predict first: a big cube is made of 4 × 4 × 4 small cubes and its whole outside is painted. How many small cubes have no paint at all?
2. Sort the small cubes by where they sit: corners, edges, face middles and inside.
3. A corner cube touches 3 faces of the big cube, so it has 3 painted faces. A cube has 8 corners.
4. An edge cube that is not a corner has 2 painted faces. Each edge has 4 − 2 = 2 of them, and a cube has 12 edges.
5. A face middle cube has 1 painted face. Each face has 2 × 2 = 4 of them, and a cube has 6 faces.
6. An inside cube touches no outside face. Take away the outer layer all round and 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cubes are left inside.
7. Rule: corners 3 faces, edges 2 faces, face middles 1 face, inside none, and the four counts add up to all the small cubes.

content.text:
Worked example: A big cube is made of 4 × 4 × 4 small cubes and all of its outside is painted. How many small cubes have 3, 2, 1 and 0 painted faces?
1. Count all the small cubes: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.
2. 3 painted faces: the corners. A cube has 8 corners, so 8 small cubes.
3. 2 painted faces: the edge cubes that are not corners. Each edge has 4 − 2 = 2 of them and there are 12 edges: 12 × 2 = 24 small cubes.
4. 1 painted face: the face middle cubes. Each face has 2 × 2 = 4 of them and there are 6 faces: 6 × 4 = 24 small cubes.
5. 0 painted faces: the cubes inside. Take off the outer layer: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 small cubes.
6. Check: 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64, all the small cubes.
Answer: 3 faces: 8 small cubes. 2 faces: 24. 1 face: 24. No face: 8. Together 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64

media.title: Cube Lab

tool_config.title: Cube Lab
tool_config.idea: Turn a cube and fold a net to say which faces are opposite, then paint and remove small cubes to count how many have three, two, one or no painted faces and how many are left in a cube frame.
tool_config.screen: A cube, a net and small cubes on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3-D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Three tabs at the top of the table switch between the Cube and net bench, the Paint bench and the Frame bench. On the Cube and net bench a big cube with a picture on each face is the largest thing on screen: a sun, a moon, a heart, a leaf, a star and a plain face. On the left sits a row of view cards: View 1 and View 2 from the video, and the three views of the book's question. On the right is a cross-shaped net of 6 empty squares, a row of 4 squares with one square above and one below the third square, with a tray of 6 picture tiles under it; the sixth tile can be set to show any one of the pictures. Cube and net controls: drag the cube to turn it; tap a view card to set the cube to that view; drag a picture tile onto a net square and tap the turn button to turn the picture; Fold folds the net into a cube and Unfold opens it. Cube and net read-outs: a line that names the three faces you can see, and, after Fold, a match light on each view card that says match or not yet with the reason. On the Paint bench a stack of small cubes (5 by 5 by 5 for practice values, 3 by 3 by 3 for the book's question) has a Paint button that paints the outside red, a Peel button that takes off one outer layer at a time, and a tap on any small cube lifts it out into one of four tally boxes: three painted faces, two, one and none. Paint bench read-outs: the number of small cubes in the stack and the number in each tally box. On the Frame bench a stack of small cubes (6 by 6 by 6, practice values) has a tunnel width control and a Cut tunnels button that removes a square tunnel through every pair of opposite faces; read-outs: the cubes removed and the cubes left. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (unfolds the net or puts back the last cubes), Reset (clears the bench), Back and Next sit in the same places on every card.
student_does: Look at View 1 and View 2 of the cube from the video, with the sun, the moon, the heart and the leaf, and at the 4 by 4 by 4 cube with 64 small cubes. Say which faces touch the heart.
Turn the cube and find the face opposite the heart, fold a net, and paint and peel a stack of small cubes. Then cut a tunnel through a frame and count what is removed.
The book's own questions. Here are three views of a cube. Can you draw them on the net in the correct order? Then Nisha's 27 small cubes painted red.
challenges: Card 1: tap View 1 and View 2 and turn the cube. Which face is opposite the heart? Answer: the moon. Both the heart and the moon touch the sun and the leaf.

Card 2 (practice values): drop the six pictures on the net: the heart, the leaf, the moon and the plain face along the row of 4 squares from left to right, the sun above the third square and the star below it. Press Fold. Which faces are opposite? Answer: the cube matches View 1 and View 2. The heart and the moon have one square between them in the row, so they are opposite, and so are the leaf and the plain face. The sun above and the star below the third square are opposite too.

Card 3 (practice values): on the Paint bench take the 5 by 5 by 5 stack, press Paint, then Peel and sort the small cubes. How many have three, two, one and no painted faces? Answer: 8, 36, 54 and 27, because 12 × 3 = 36, 6 × 9 = 54 and 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, and 8 + 36 + 54 + 27 = 125.

Card 4 (practice values): on the Frame bench take the 6 by 6 by 6 stack and cut a tunnel 4 by 4 through every pair of opposite faces. How many small cubes are removed? Answer: 160. What is left is the 8 corners and 4 cubes on each of the 12 edges, 8 + 12 × 4 = 56, and 6 × 6 × 6 = 216, so 216 − 56 = 160 are removed.

Challenge: 'Here are three views of a cube. Can you draw them on the net in the correct order?' Answer: the diamond face is opposite the brown face, the circle face is opposite the star face, and the cross is on two opposite faces. Sample net: a row of 4 squares with the brown face, the circle, the diamond and the star from left to right, and a cross above and below the diamond square. Your net may differ if it keeps the same opposite faces.

Challenge: 'Nisha has glued 27 small cubes together to make a large solid cube. She paints the large cube red. How many of the original small cubes have (a) three faces painted red? (b) two faces painted red? (c) one face painted red? (d) no faces painted red?' Answer: (a) 8, (b) 12, (c) 6 and (d) 1, because 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27.
feedback: After Fold the tool says which views match, for example: View 1 matches. In View 2 the leaf and the moon should be next to the sun: look at what touches the sun.
When you turn the cube the tool names the faces you see and says: Faces you see together touch each other, so they cannot be opposite.
Both the heart and the moon touch the sun and the leaf: they are opposite. The tool shows this when the two views are set one after the other.

On the Paint bench a small cube lifted into the wrong tally box slides back with a clue such as: Count the painted faces of this cube. How many outside faces does it touch? The cube hidden in the middle has none.

On the Frame bench the tool says how many were removed and how many are left, and a count that does not add up gets a soft amber note, for example: Removed and left must make 216. A wrong answer is never shown in red.
tool_config.done_when: The student has turned the cube to find the opposite of the heart, folded the net, sorted a painted stack, cut a tunnel in a frame, placed the book's three views on a net and sorted Nisha's 27 small cubes by painted faces.

hint_ladder.text: Which faces can you see together in one view? Faces seen together touch each other. For small cubes, ask how many outside faces a cube touches.
Opposite faces never touch and are never seen together. Look for two faces that touch the same two touching faces. For small cubes, sort them: corner, edge, face middle, inside.
Turn the cube to the view you need and name the faces you see. For small cubes, count the corners, then the cubes on each edge, then the cubes in the middle of a face, then the cubes inside.

The tool places one picture on the net, the diamond in the third square of the row, so you can see how the other pictures fit round it. For small cubes it peels off the outer layer so you can count the cubes left inside.

media.description: Concept video: Show how three views of a cube tell which faces are opposite and how a net folds. It works this example: A cube has six faces: sun, moon, heart, leaf, star and a plain face. In View 1 the sun is on top, the heart is on the left and the leaf is on the right. In View 2 the sun is on top, the leaf is on the left and the moon is on the right. Which face is opposite the heart?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: in one view of a cube the heart touches the sun and the leaf. In another view the moon touches the sun and the leaf. Which face is opposite the heart? Faces that you see together in one view touch each other, so they are not opposite. Opposite faces are never seen together. The heart touches the sun and the leaf. The moon also touches the sun and the leaf. The sun and the leaf touch each other along one edge, and the two faces at the two ends of that edge are opposite. So the heart is opposite the moon. A net is a cube cut open and laid flat: 6 squares joined by their sides. In a straight row of 3 squares, the first and the third fold up to opposite faces. Rule: two faces that both touch the same two touching faces are opposite each other. 1. View 1: the heart touches the sun and the leaf. 2. View 2: the moon touches the sun and the leaf. 3. So the heart and the moon both touch the same two faces, the sun and the leaf. 4. The sun and the leaf touch each other along one edge. The two faces at the two ends of that edge are opposite each other, and they are the heart and the moon. 5. So the heart is opposite the moon. 6. Check: opposite faces are never seen together. The heart is in View 1 and the moon is in View 2, and they never appear in the same view. Answer: The moon is opposite the heart

media.description: Concept video: Show how to count the small cubes of a big painted cube by corners, edges, faces and inside. It works this example: A big cube is made of 4 × 4 × 4 small cubes and all of its outside is painted. How many small cubes have 3, 2, 1 and 0 painted faces?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a big cube is made of 4 × 4 × 4 small cubes and its whole outside is painted. How many small cubes have no paint at all? Sort the small cubes by where they sit: corners, edges, face middles and inside. A corner cube touches 3 faces of the big cube, so it has 3 painted faces. A cube has 8 corners. An edge cube that is not a corner has 2 painted faces. Each edge has 4 − 2 = 2 of them, and a cube has 12 edges. A face middle cube has 1 painted face. Each face has 2 × 2 = 4 of them, and a cube has 6 faces. An inside cube touches no outside face. Take away the outer layer all round and 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cubes are left inside. Rule: corners 3 faces, edges 2 faces, face middles 1 face, inside none, and the four counts add up to all the small cubes. 1. Count all the small cubes: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. 2. 3 painted faces: the corners. A cube has 8 corners, so 8 small cubes. 3. 2 painted faces: the edge cubes that are not corners. Each edge has 4 − 2 = 2 of them and there are 12 edges: 12 × 2 = 24 small cubes. 4. 1 painted face: the face middle cubes. Each face has 2 × 2 = 4 of them and there are 6 faces: 6 × 4 = 24 small cubes. 5. 0 painted faces: the cubes inside. Take off the outer layer: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 small cubes. 6. Check: 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64, all the small cubes. Answer: 3 faces: 8 small cubes. 2 faces: 24. 1 face: 24. No face: 8. Together 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64

steps: Name the pictures: a green diamond on purple, an orange circle on blue, a red cross on cream, a blue star on pink, and a plain brown face.
Faces seen together in one view touch each other, so they are next to each other and not opposite.
The diamond face and the brown face both touch the circle face and the cross face, so the diamond is opposite the brown face.
The circle face and the star face both touch the diamond face and the cross face, so the circle is opposite the star.
A cube has 6 faces: diamond, brown, circle, star and two more. The third view shows a cross next to the circle and the brown face, so the cross must be on two opposite faces.

Draw the net: a row of 4 squares with the brown face, the circle, the diamond and the star from left to right, then a cross above the diamond square and a cross below it. Turn each picture so it looks as it does in the views.

Check: in the row, brown and diamond have one square between them, and so do circle and star, so each pair is opposite. The two crosses are above and below the diamond square, so they are opposite too.

content.book_number: Cube Connections: cube frames
content.question: Here are some big solid cube frames. How many small cubes have been removed from each cube? (a), (b), (c)
steps: (a): the cube is 3 by 3 by 3, so it has 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 small cubes.
A square tunnel goes through the middle of every pair of opposite faces. What is left is the 8 corners and 1 cube on each of the 12 edges: 8 + 12 × 1 = 20. Removed: 27 − 20 = 7.
(b): the cube is 4 by 4 by 4, so it has 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 small cubes. Left: the 8 corners and 2 cubes on each of the 12 edges: 8 + 12 × 2 = 32. Removed: 64 − 32 = 32.
(c): the cube is 5 by 5 by 5, so it has 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 small cubes. Left: the 8 corners and 3 cubes on each of the 12 edges: 8 + 12 × 3 = 44. Removed: 125 − 44 = 81.
content.answer: (a): 7 small cubes; (b): 32 small cubes; (c): 81 small cubes.
content.text:
1. $(a)$: the cube is $3$ by $3$ by $3$, so it has $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ small cubes.
2. A square tunnel goes through the middle of every pair of opposite faces. What is left is the $8$ corners and $1$ cube on each of the $12$ edges: $8 + 12 \times 1 = 20$. Removed: $27 - 20 = 7$.
[Image: Cube Connections: Ans2: solution]
3. $(b)$: the cube is $4$ by $4$ by $4$, so it has $4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$ small cubes. Left: the $8$ corners and $2$ cubes on each of the $12$ edges: $8 + 12 \times 2 = 32$. Removed: $64 - 32 = 32$.
4. $(c)$: the cube is $5$ by $5$ by $5$, so it has $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$ small cubes. Left: the $8$ corners and $3$ cubes on each of the $12$ edges: $8 + 12 \times 3 = 44$. Removed: $125 - 44 = 81$.
5. Check: $20 + 7 = 27$, $32 + 32 = 64$ and $44 + 81 = 125$.
Answer: $(a)$: $7$ small cubes; $(b)$: $32$ small cubes; $(c)$: $81$ small cubes.
[Image: Cube Connections: Ans2: solution (continued)]

concepts.concept_name: Solving a Shape Puzzle with Clues

content.text:
1. Predict first: five shapes stand in a line and one clue says the circle is at the left end. Which clue do you use first?
2. Start with the clue that gives a sure place. The circle is at the left end, so the circle goes first.
3. Then use each clue to fill the next place. Draw empty boxes and write each shape in its box as you place it.
4. When a clue says a shape is between two others, it sits directly between them.
5. At the end read every clue again and check it against the finished line.
6. Rule: place what is surest first, then use each clue to fill the next place.

content.text:
Worked example: Nisha puts 5 shapes in a line: a circle, a square, a triangle, a hexagon and a rectangle. Clues: (a) The circle is at the left end. (b) The square is next to the circle. (c) The triangle is between the square and the hexagon. (d) The rectangle is to the right of the hexagon. In what order are the shapes?
1. Draw 5 boxes in a line, numbered 1 to 5 from the left.
2. Clue (a): the circle is at the left end, so the circle is in box 1.
3. Clue (b): the square is next to the circle. Box 1 is the circle, so the square is in box 2.
4. Clue (c): the triangle is between the square and the hexagon. The square is in box 2, so the triangle is in box 3 and the hexagon is in box 4.
5. Clue (d): the rectangle is to the right of the hexagon. Box 5 is the only box to the right of box 4, so the rectangle is in box 5.
6. Check: the line is circle, square, triangle, hexagon, rectangle. Clue (a): the circle is at the left end, yes. Clue (b): the square is next to the circle, yes. Clue (c): the triangle is between the square and the hexagon, yes. Clue (d): the rectangle is to the right of the hexagon, yes.
Answer: From left to right: circle, square, triangle, hexagon, rectangle

(c): The two triangles are next to the square. (d): The hexagon is to the right of the triangle. (e): The circle is to the left of the square.
steps: Draw 7 boxes in a line. The shapes are 2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon and 1 rectangle, and 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 7.
Clues (a) and (e): the square is directly between the circle and the rectangle, and the circle is to the left of the square. So three shapes sit side by side: circle, square, rectangle.
Clue (b): the rectangle is between the square and the triangle. The square is on its left, so a triangle is on its right: circle, square, rectangle, triangle.

Clue (c): the two triangles are next to the square. The first square already has the circle and the rectangle beside it, so the triangles are on both sides of the other square: triangle, square, triangle. One triangle is already placed, so the line goes on with square, triangle: circle, square, rectangle, triangle, square, triangle.
Clue (d): the hexagon is to the right of the triangle. The only shape left is the hexagon, and it goes at the right end: circle, square, rectangle, triangle, square, triangle, hexagon.

Check: there are 2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon and 1 rectangle. Clue (a): the square in box 2 is between the circle and the rectangle, yes. Clue (b): the rectangle in box 3 is between the square and the triangle, yes. Clue (c): the triangles in boxes 4 and 6 are next to the square in box 5, yes. Clue (d): the hexagon is to the right of the triangle, yes. Clue (e): the circle is to the left of the square, yes.

concepts.concept_name: Faces and Corners of a Solid

content.text:
1. Predict first: a matchbox is a solid. How many faces does it have, and how many corners? Count every one only once.
2. A face is a flat side of a solid. The box has 6 faces, and all of them are rectangles. Opposite faces are the same.
3. A vertex is a point where faces meet. It is the corner of the solid. At every vertex of the box, 3 faces meet.
4. Count the vertices the same way, ticking each one once. The box has 8 vertices.
5. Models of solids such as the icosahedron and the dodecahedron can be made from nets, or built from straws and clay. You count their faces and vertices in the same way.
6. Rule: count face by face and tick each one; a vertex is a point where faces meet.

content.text:
Worked example: A matchbox is a solid. How many faces does it have and what shape are they? How many faces meet at each vertex? How many vertices does it have?
1. Hold the box and tick each face once: top, bottom, front, back, left and right.
2. That makes 6 faces. Every face is a rectangle, and opposite faces are the same.
3. Look at one corner. A vertex is a point where faces meet. At this vertex 3 faces meet: the top, the front and the right.
4. Every vertex of the box looks the same, so 3 faces meet at every vertex.
5. Count the vertices: 4 on the top face and 4 on the bottom face, so 4 + 4 = 8.
6. Check: ticking each face and each vertex once gives 6 faces and 8 vertices, with none missed and none counted twice.
Answer: The box has 6 faces, all rectangles. 3 faces meet at every vertex, and it has 8 vertices

concepts.concept_name: Counting the Edges of a Solid

content.text:
1. Predict first: the box has 6 faces and each face has 4 sides. If you add up all the sides, do you get the number of edges?
2. An edge is a line where two faces meet. Count the sides of every face: 6 × 4 = 24 sides.
3. But each edge is a side of 2 faces, so every edge was counted twice.
4. So halve the count: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 edges.
5. Check by counting the edges another way: 4 round the top, 4 round the bottom and 4 standing up between them, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
6. Rule: count the sides of all the faces, then halve, because each edge belongs to 2 faces.

content.text:
Worked example: A box has 6 faces and each face has 4 sides. How many edges does the box have? How can you count them without missing an edge or counting one twice?
1. Count the sides of all the faces: 6 faces with 4 sides each, 6 × 4 = 24 sides.
2. An edge is the line where 2 faces meet, so every edge is a side of 2 faces.
3. So the 24 sides count every edge twice. Halve the count: 24 ÷ 2 = 12 edges.
4. Check another way: 4 edges round the top, 4 round the bottom and 4 standing up between them, so 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Answer: The box has 12 edges. Count the sides of all the faces, 6 × 4 = 24, then halve it: 24 ÷ 2 = 12

tool_config.title: Solid Counter
tool_config.idea: Tick the faces, vertices and edges of a box and then of the icosahedron and the dodecahedron, one tick for each, and find the number of edges by adding the sides of all the faces and halving, so that nothing is missed and nothing is counted twice.
tool_config.screen: A turntable on the craft table with clay models, drawn as a warm 3-D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The solid on the turntable is the largest thing on screen. Three model cards on the left choose the solid: Box, Icosahedron and Dodecahedron. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag the turntable to turn the solid so that every side can be seen; a mode switch with Faces, Vertices and Edges that chooses what a tap ticks; tap a face, a vertex or an edge to tick it with an amber mark and tap it again to take the tick off; a Tally button that opens a strip adding the sides of every ticked face, and a Halve button on that strip; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the ticks of this card), Reset (clears the solid), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: three counters, faces ticked, vertices ticked and edges ticked; a faces at this vertex read-out that lights up the faces touching a ticked vertex and shows their number; the sides tally, for example 6 faces × 4 sides = 24, and the halved number under it; and a line that says whether any face, vertex or edge is still unticked.
student_does: Look at the box from the video. Tick each of its faces once and say how many faces and how many vertices it has, and how many faces meet at a vertex.
Count the edges of the box by adding the sides of all the faces and halving, then switch to the icosahedron and the dodecahedron and tick their faces.
The book's own questions. How many faces meet at a vertex (point)? Then: How many edges do you see? How did you count them such that you do not miss out any edge or count an edge twice?
challenges: Card 1: on the box choose Faces and tap each face once. How many faces are there, and what shape are they? Answer: 6 faces, all rectangles.

Card 2: on the box choose Vertices and tap one vertex, then count all the vertices. How many faces meet at a vertex, and how many vertices are there? Answer: 3 faces meet at every vertex, and the box has 8 vertices.
Card 3: on the box press Tally, then Halve. How many edges does the box have? Answer: 6 × 4 = 24 sides, and 24 ÷ 2 = 12 edges.
Card 4: switch to the icosahedron, choose Faces and tick every face. How many faces, and what shape are they? Answer: 20 faces, all triangles.
Card 5: switch to the dodecahedron, choose Faces and tick every face. How many faces, and what shape are they? Answer: 12 faces, all pentagons.

Challenge: 'How many faces meet at a vertex (point)?' Tap vertices on the icosahedron and on the dodecahedron and compare. Answer: the icosahedron has 5 faces at a vertex and the dodecahedron has 3, and the same number of faces meet at every vertex of each solid.

Challenge: 'How many edges do you see? How did you count them such that you do not miss out any edge or count an edge twice?' Answer: 30 edges in each solid. Add the sides of all the faces, 20 × 3 = 60 for the icosahedron and 12 × 5 = 60 for the dodecahedron, then halve it, because each edge is a side of 2 faces: 60 ÷ 2 = 30.

The Tally strip adds the sides of the ticked faces and says, for example: 20 faces with 3 sides is 60. Every edge is counted twice, so halve it: 30 edges.
When every face is ticked the tool says: All 20 faces are counted, none is missed. If one is still unticked it turns the solid to show where it is and says: One face is still hidden at the back.
A wrong count shows a soft amber note and never a red cross; the tool names the number it expected only after the second try.

media.teaching_notes: 1. Count the sides of all the faces. Icosahedron: 20 faces with 3 sides each, so 20 × 3 = 60 sides. 2. Dodecahedron: 12 faces with 5 sides each, so 12 × 5 = 60 sides. 3. Check: every edge is shared by exactly 2 faces, so no edge is missed and none is counted twice. Answer: Icosahedron: 30 edges; Dodecahedron: 30 edges. content.text:
1. Predict first: you have walked round the whole craft table. Can you say one idea from each stop, from the woven mat to the solids? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Weaving: write a row as steps with over and under, then say repeat. A row can be 3 over, 2 under (repeat). The next row can swap over and under. The pattern repeats when a row is the same as Row 1.
3. Check: Row 1 is 1 over, 2 under (repeat) and each next row starts one step later. Row 4 is the same as Row 1, so the rows repeat after 3 rows.
4. Tiling: shapes with all sides equal are regular shapes. Regular triangles, squares and hexagons fit round a point with no gap and no overlap, so they tessellate. Regular pentagons and regular octagons leave a gap that is too small, so they do not.
5. Check: why can five squares not fit round a point? Four squares already fill the space, so a fifth would overlap.
6. Patterns with two shapes: at a point, list the shapes that meet. In a pattern that repeats, the same set of shapes meets at every point.
7. Triangles: an isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides and 2 equal angles, an equilateral triangle has all 3 sides and all 3 angles equal, and a scalene triangle has no equal sides. Fold a triangle to compare its angles.
8. Check: a triangle has sides 8, 8 and 3. It has 2 equal sides, so it is isosceles.
9. Four-sided shapes: a kite has adjacent sides equal, a parallelogram has opposite sides equal, and a rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles.
10. Check: a four-sided shape has sides 5, 5, 3, 3 in order. The equal sides are next to each other, so it is a kite.
11. Tangram: the seven pieces are 5 triangles and 2 four-sided shapes, 5 + 2 = 7. Square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram all have opposite sides equal; angles and the other sides tell them apart.
12. Circles: join the ends of two diameters and you always get a rectangle; if the diameters cross at a right angle all four sides are equal, a square. Joining points on a circle one after another makes a string design.
13. Check: on a circle of 12 points, joining 1 to 5, 5 to 2, 2 to 6 and so on until you are back at 1 takes 17 lines.
14. Cubes: two faces that touch the same two neighbouring faces are opposite. A big cube of 4 by 4 by 4 small cubes painted outside has 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64 small cubes: 8 with three painted faces, 24 with two, 24 with one and 8 with none.
15. Puzzle and solids: place the surest shape first and use each clue in turn. To count the edges of a solid, count the sides of all its faces and halve the total, because every edge is the side of 2 faces.
16. Check: a box has 6 faces with 4 sides each, 6 × 4 = 24 sides, and 24 ÷ 2 = 12 edges.

12. Circles: join the ends of two diameters and you always get a rectangle; if the diameters cross at a right angle all four sides are equal, a square. Joining points on a circle one after another makes a string design.
13. Check: on a circle of 12 points, joining 1 to 5, 5 to 2, 2 to 6 and so on until you are back at 1 takes 17 lines.
14. Cubes: two faces that touch the same two neighbouring faces are opposite. A big cube of 4 by 4 by 4 small cubes painted outside has 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64 small cubes: 8 with three painted faces, 24 with two, 24 with one and 8 with none.
15. Puzzle and solids: place the surest shape first and use each clue in turn. To count the edges of a solid, count the sides of all its faces and halve the total, because every edge is the side of 2 faces.
16. Check: a box has 6 faces with 4 sides each, 6 × 4 = 24 sides, and 24 ÷ 2 = 12 edges.
steps: Predict first: you have walked round the whole craft table. Can you say one idea from each stop, from the woven mat to the solids? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
Weaving: write a row as steps with over and under, then say repeat. A row can be 3 over, 2 under (repeat). The next row can swap over and under. The pattern repeats when a row is the same as Row 1.
Check: Row 1 is 1 over, 2 under (repeat) and each next row starts one step later. Row 4 is the same as Row 1, so the rows repeat after 3 rows.

Tiling: shapes with all sides equal are regular shapes. Regular triangles, squares and hexagons fit round a point with no gap and no overlap, so they tessellate. Regular pentagons and regular octagons leave a gap that is too small, so they do not.
Check: why can five squares not fit round a point? Four squares already fill the space, so a fifth would overlap.
Patterns with two shapes: at a point, list the shapes that meet. In a pattern that repeats, the same set of shapes meets at every point.

Triangles: an isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides and 2 equal angles, an equilateral triangle has all 3 sides and all 3 angles equal, and a scalene triangle has no equal sides. Fold a triangle to compare its angles.
Check: a triangle has sides 8, 8 and 3. It has 2 equal sides, so it is isosceles.
Four-sided shapes: a kite has adjacent sides equal, a parallelogram has opposite sides equal, and a rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles.
Check: a four-sided shape has sides 5, 5, 3, 3 in order. The equal sides are next to each other, so it is a kite.
Tangram: the seven pieces are 5 triangles and 2 four-sided shapes, 5 + 2 = 7. Square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram all have opposite sides equal; angles and the other sides tell them apart.

Circles: join the ends of two diameters and you always get a rectangle; if the diameters cross at a right angle all four sides are equal, a square. Joining points on a circle one after another makes a string design.
Check: on a circle of 12 points, joining 1 to 5, 5 to 2, 2 to 6 and so on until you are back at 1 takes 17 lines.

Cubes: two faces that touch the same two neighbouring faces are opposite. A big cube of 4 by 4 by 4 small cubes painted outside has 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64 small cubes: 8 with three painted faces, 24 with two, 24 with one and 8 with none.

Puzzle and solids: place the surest shape first and use each clue in turn. To count the edges of a solid, count the sides of all its faces and halve the total, because every edge is the side of 2 faces.
Check: a box has 6 faces with 4 sides each, 6 × 4 = 24 sides, and 24 ÷ 2 = 12 edges.

objectives.objective_text: Students describe one row of a weave in words by counting the over and under steps and saying repeat, and write the next row by swapping over and under.
Students write the rows of a weave until a row is the same as Row 1, and say after how many rows the pattern repeats.
Students build rows of a weave from rules of over and under steps, and find the row where the pattern starts to repeat.
Students sort shapes into regular and not regular by comparing the lengths of their sides, and name a regular pentagon and a regular octagon.
Students decide whether copies of a shape fill the space round a point with no gap and no overlap, and say that such a shape tessellates.
Students fit regular triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons and octagons around a point and say which fit with no gap and no overlap.
Students list the shapes that meet at the joins of a border made of two shapes that take turns, and say whether the same set of shapes meets at every join.
Students continue a pattern made of two shapes on a dot grid, and list the shapes that meet at a marked point.
Students name an isosceles triangle by its 2 equal sides, and fold it in half to show that it also has 2 equal angles.
Students name a triangle as equilateral, isosceles or scalene from the lengths of its sides, and say how many of its angles are equal.
Students make triangles from the pieces of a rhombus, measure their sides and fold them, and say whether each triangle is equilateral, isosceles or scalene.
Students tell a kite from a parallelogram by checking whether the equal sides are next to each other or opposite each other.
Students name a four-sided shape with equal opposite sides as a parallelogram, and tell a rectangle from other parallelograms by its right angles.
Students join 2, 3 and 4 pieces of the rhombus side to side, count the sides of each shape made, and name the four-sided shapes by their sides and angles.
Students sort the 7 tangram pieces by their number of sides, and name each piece as a small, medium or large triangle, a square or a parallelogram.
Students name the seven tangram pieces, say how they are the same or different, and make shapes from some or all of the pieces in more than one way.
Students name a four-sided shape as a square, rectangle, rhombus or parallelogram by checking its sides and its angles, and say which statements fit more than one of these shapes.
Students match seven statements about sides and angles with the square, rectangle, rhombus or parallelogram they describe, and find which statements fit more than one shape.
Students join the ends of two diameters of a circle and name the shape formed by checking its sides and its angles.
Students join points round a circle by a repeating move, such as on by 4 and back by 3, and count the lines when the thread is back at the start.
Students draw two diameters of a circle, join the ends and check the shape, and thread the points of a circle to make a string design.
Students use two views of a cube to name the face opposite a given face and say which clue they used.
Students sort the small cubes of a big painted cube into corners, edges, face middles and inside, and count how many have three, two, one or no painted faces.
Students find opposite faces of a cube, place pictures on a net, and count painted and removed small cubes in a cube frame and in a painted cube.
Students place five shapes in a line by using each clue in turn, starting with the surest clue, and check every clue against the finished line.
Students place seven shapes in a line by using five clues one at a time, and check every clue against the finished line.
Students count the faces and vertices of a solid by ticking each one once, and say how many faces meet at a vertex.
Students count the edges of a solid by adding the sides of all its faces and halving the total, because each edge is the side of two faces.
Students count the faces, vertices and edges of each solid, the icosahedron and the dodecahedron, and say how many faces meet at each vertex.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Can you figure out how to make this mat? Let us try to understand how this mat is woven by looking at the pattern in the first two rows. Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... Row 2: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, 1 over, ... You can use strips of the same colour or 2 different colours, one for each row.

Book item: Try to weave a pattern, using the rules given below. Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). Row 2: 1 under (do not repeat), 3 over, 3 under, 3 over, 3 under, ... (repeat). Row 3: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, ... (repeat). Row 4: 1 over (do not repeat), 3 under, 3 over, ... (repeat). Continue weaving in this order.
Book item: Can you work out the steps for any of these designs and weave the pattern? Write the steps of the pattern in your notebook for each row until it starts repeating.
Book item: Draw the following pattern on a grid paper. Part of it is done for you. Now, complete the rest of the grid to get the full design.
Book item: We have placed 3 pentagons around a point. Can we fit one more into the empty space?
Book item: Can regular triangles fit together at a point without any gap? How many of them fit together?
Book item: Can squares (a regular 4-sided shape) fit together around a point without any gap or overlap? Try it out using cutouts of squares. How many squares did you need?
Book item: Can five squares fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?
Book item: Can regular hexagons (6-sided shapes with equal sides) fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Try and see. How many fit together at a point?
Book item: Do regular octagons fit together without any gaps or overlaps? Try drawing the same and check.
Book item: Here is a tessellating pattern with more than one shape. What shapes have been used in this pattern? ___, ___.
Book item: Continue the pattern given below and colour it appropriately.

Book item: Look at the pattern given below. What shapes are coming together at the marked points? Are the same set of shapes coming together at these points? Continue the pattern and colour it appropriately.
Book item: Here is a tiling pattern made using two different shapes, squares and triangles. Are the triangles equilateral? Why or why not?
Book item: What shapes are coming together at the marked points? Are the same set of shapes coming together at these points? Continue the pattern and colour it appropriately.
Book item: Create similar patterns using other cutouts of shapes.
Book item: What geometrical shapes can you make by fitting 2 of these triangles together? Trace the shapes you created.
Book item: How many different types of triangles can you make? Now, observe and measure the sides of these triangles. What do you notice?
Book item: Trace the isosceles triangles on a paper and cut them out. Fold them in half. What do you notice about their angles?
Book item: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal (equilateral triangle)?
Book item: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal?
Book item: Take an equilateral triangle. Check if all the angles of an equilateral triangle are equal, just like you did with the isosceles triangle.
Book item: Now, cut the equilateral triangle in half. How many sides of each new triangle are equal?
Book item: Check in scalene triangles whether any two or more angles are equal?
Book item: How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make?
Book item: Measure the sides of each of these two quadrilaterals A and B. What do you notice? Are there any pairs of sides that are equal? Which pairs are equal, adjacent or opposite?
Book item: What types of angles do quadrilaterals A and B have? Which angles are equal in each of the above parallelograms?
Book item: In the grid given below, draw two different kites and parallelograms each.

Book item: Now, use 3 triangles from the rhombus to form shapes. How many sides do each one of them have? Using 3 triangular pieces of the rhombus, try creating: (a): a 3-sided shape; (b): a 4-sided shape; (c): a 5-sided shape.
Book item: Which of these shapes can be made with all 4 pieces? Try and find out. (a): Square; (b): Rectangle; (c): Triangle; (d): Pentagon, 5-sided; (e): Hexagon, 6-sided; (f): Octagon, 8-sided

Book item: Make your own kite shape. (a): Start with a square piece of paper. (b): Take one corner of the paper and fold it towards the opposite corner, creating a sharp crease along the diagonal. (c): Open and fold the corner A inwards, aligning the edge with the crease you just made. (d): Repeat on the other side, folding the other corner B inwards to align with the crease at the centre. You have a kite shape! What shapes do you see in the kite?
Book item: Look at the tangram set. Cut out all the shapes. Name them.
Book item: (a): How are they same or different from each other?
Book item: (b): What do you notice about the angles of each of the shapes?
Book item: (c): What do you notice about the sides of each of the shapes?
Book item: Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it.

Book item: Match the statements with appropriate shapes. Do some of them describe more than one shape? (1): All my angles are right angles, but all my sides are not equal. (2): All my sides are equal, but all my angles are not. (3): My opposite angles are equal, but my sides do not make a right angle. (4): Two pairs of sides are equal, but they do not make a right angle. (5): All my sides make right angles with each other and are equal. (6): My opposite angles are equal and so are my sides. (7): My opposite angles are equal and my sides make right angles. The shapes: Square, Rectangle, Rhombus, Parallelogram.

Book item: (a): Draw a circle with a compass and mark its centre. (b): Draw its diameter. Mark the endpoints of the diameter. (c): Draw another diameter of the circle and mark the endpoints. (d): Now join the four points. What shape is formed? Check the sides of the quadrilateral and the angles obtained.
Book item: Try with a different pair of diameters. What do you notice about the shape that is formed?
Book item: Is it possible to create a 4-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process?
Book item: Look at the circle given below. It is marked with points 1 to 24. Join points 1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, and so on till you reach back at 1.
Book item: Can you think of a way to make a design exactly like the image given here? Try to make it.
Book item: Here are three views of a cube. Can you draw them on the net in the correct order?
Book item: Here are some big solid cube frames. How many small cubes have been removed from each cube? (a), (b), (c)

Book item: Nisha has glued 27 small cubes together to make a large solid cube. She paints the large cube red. How many of the original small cubes have (a): three faces painted red? ___; (b): two faces painted red? ___; (c): one face painted red? ___; (d): no faces painted red? ___

Book item: Tanu arranged 7 shapes in a line. She used 2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, and 1 rectangle. Find her arrangement using the following clues: (a): The square is between the circle and the rectangle. (b): The rectangle is between the square and the triangle. (c): The two triangles are next to the square. (d): The hexagon is to the right of the triangle. (e): The circle is to the left of the square.
Book item: What do these names mean? Once you count their faces, you will know.
Book item: What shapes do you see in an icosahedron and a dodecahedron? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___ Do all the faces look the same? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___
Book item: How many faces meet at a vertex (point)? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___ Do the same number of faces meet at each vertex? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___
Book item: How many edges do you see? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___ How did you count them such that you do not miss out any edge or count an edge twice?
Book item: Can you think of any other solid shapes that have faces that look the same? Do the same number of faces meet at each common vertex?
Book item: You can also build some solid shapes using straws or ice-cream sticks and clay or play dough. Which shapes did you make?
